subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS

speechtext:
Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) moved the second reading of Bill No. 2, to readjust the representation in the House of Commons.
He said: In moving the second reading of Bill No. 2, to readjust the representation in the House of Commons, I think it is necessary only to point out that the bill corresponds identically, except as to dates, with chapter 63 of the statutes of 1924. It is identical also with the bill introduced by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) in 1923 when Prime Minister, except as to section 4 which has been amended to meet the changed conditions with respect to population. It might be pointed out that the practice of introducing this bill in this form commenced in 1903 when the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier brought in a bill which set forth the number of members to which the provinces would be entitled under redistribution, it being left- to the house to determine the boundaries of the constituencies. This matter was very fully dealt with by the right hon. gentleman opposite when he introduced a bill in 1923, and I do not think any good purpose will be served by repeating the statements then made except to say that the practice commenced by Sir Wilfried Laurier in 1903 has been followed in subsequent redistribution measures. The old contest in the House of Commons over the boundaries of constituencies which

Redistribution-Mr. Bennett
represented the views of the government of the day, has not taken place since 1903. In this instance, it is proposed to proceed exactly as has been done since 1903.
It will be recalled that the British North America Act provided that ait Confederation the number of members in the House of Commons would be 181-this is covered by section 37-and that the method by which increases were to be made as provided by the constitution is covered by section 51, which reads:
On the completion of the census in the year cue thousand eight hundred and seventy-one, and of each subsequent decennial census, the representation of the four provinces shall be readjusted by such authority, in such manner, and from such time as the parliament of Canada from time to time provides, subject and according to the following rules:
(1)	Quebec shall have a fixed number of sixty-five members;
(2)	There shall be assigned to each of the other provinces such a number of members as will bear the same proportion to tile number of its population (ascertained at such census) as the number sixty-five bears to the number of the population of Quebec (so ascertained) ;
(3)	In the computation of the number of members for a province a fractional part not exceeding one-half of the whole number requisite for entitling the province to a member shall be disregarded; but a fractional part exceeding one-half of that number shall be equivalent to the whole number;
(4)	On any such readjustment the number of members for a province shall not be reduced unless the proportion which the number of the population of the province bore to the number of the aggregate population of Canada at the then last preceding readjustment of the number of members for the province is ascertained at the then latest census to be diminished by one-twentieth part or upwards;
(5)	Such readjustment shall not take effect until the termination of the then existing parliament.
It will be observed that the unit of representation is ascertained by dividing sixty-five, the constant number of members from Quebec, into the population of that province. Inasmuch as the boundaries of the province of Quebec were extended in 1912, it was provided, in order that the other provinces might not feel that they had been unfairly dealt with, that the population into which sixty-five would be divided would be the population of old Quebec, that is, the population within the area of the provinces as it was at confederation. The effects of the present census are set forth in the notes to the bill. It might be well to indicate the populations of
the provinces under the census of 1931, which were as follows:
Prince Edward	Island	 88,038
Nova Scotia	 512,846
New Brunswick	 408,219
Ontario	 3,431,683
Manitoba	 700,139
Saskatchewan	 921,785
Alberta	 731,605
British Columbia	 694,263
Quebec (without	new	Quebec)..	2,872,078
The population of new Quebec is given at 2,177. The total population into which sixty-five is to be divided is 2,872,078, and the result of that division is a quotient of 44,186, which constitutes the unit of representation. By dividing the population which I have indicated for the different provinces with this unit of representation, we have the representation to which each province is entitled.
However, there are two exceptions which must be borne in mind. The first is found in subsection four of section 51 of the British North America Act, to which I have just directed attention. This deals with the diminution in population and provides that where the change in population does not exceed one-twentieth, there shall be no change, but where it does exceed one-twentieth, it is competent to reduce the number of members.
The second exception is to be found in the provisions of the constitutional amendment of 1915. It will be recalled that after Prince Edward Island came into confederation, the number of senators from the three maritime provinces remained at twenty-four. Two senators were taken from New Brunswick and two from Nova Scotia, and Prince Edward Island was then given four senators, so that Nova Scotia had ten; New Brunswick, ten and Prince Edward Island, four. But it was provided in 1915, in consequence of the representations so strongly urged in the house at that time, that a change should be. made by amending the constitution and, as a result of the amendment which was made it was provided that the representation in the House of Commons should never be less than that in the Senate. So Prince Edward Island, which would be entitled to only two members, is, by reason of the operation of that provision, entitled to four and the province of New Brunswick that would be entitled to only nine members, under the rule set forth in section 51 of the British North America Act, will be entitled to ten members because it has a representation of ten in the Senate. There-

Redistribulion-Mr. Bennett
fore the application of the rule, with the exceptions to which I have just directed attention, would result in the following;
Province-	Representation
Prince Edward Island	 4
Nova Scotia	 12
New Brunswick	 10
Quebec		65
Ontario	 82
Manitoba	 17
Saskatchewan	 21
Alberta	 17
British Columbia	 16
Yukon	 1
We have in the draft bill provided for one member for the Yukon, leaving its representation as it is. This makes a total of 245 members.
It will be further observed, from the notes that accompany the bill, that were it not for the application of the exception provided for in section 51, there would have been a loss of membership in Ontario, but inasmuch as the census indicates there has been no diminution that exceeds one-twentieth, the membership remains at eighty-two the figure we now have. The net result is that the representation of New Brunswick, as I said, will be ten instead of nine by reason of the provisions of the statute of 1915; that of Ontario will be eighty-two as it now is; that of British Columbia will be increased by two, from fourteen to sixteen; that of Alberta is increased by one, from sixteen to seventeen; that of Manitoba will be seventeen as it now is; that of Saskatchewan will be twenty-one as it now is; that of Prince Edward Island remains at four as it now is, by reason of the 1915 amendment referred to; that of Nova Scotia will be reduced from fourteen to twelve, the result being that we have a total of 245 members as the house is now constituted. I do not think it desirable to put on Hansard again the figures that have been so frequently placed there, but I wish merely to indicate the general principles that govern the redistribution and the result of the application of the rule and its exceptions.
When the bill has been read a second time, I propose to move that it be referred to a committee, the names of which I hope to indicate to the house before we adjourn, the motion being that the bill be referred to a committee to be set up, the names of which, as I say, I shall presently give, I hope possibly at three o'clock. It is thought a committee of twenty will be satisfactory, as according to the strength of the parties in the house the
J-Mr. Bennett.]
government would have eleven members, the official opposition seven, and the other groups two on that committee. That involves a fair and just application of the relative strength of the parties in the house to a committee of twenty.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the statement by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) to the effect that the government intends to follow with respect to the readjustment of representation in this bouse about to be effected procedure similar to that which has been followed in the last three distributions, is entirely satisfactory. My right hon. friend says that the present bill is, with one exception which he has mentioned, identical with that which was presented to the house by the previous administration at the time of the last redistribution. That, I believe, is also correct and the fact may I say, quite satisfactory as far as we are concerned. In following the same procedure I hope it will be understood -and I assume it is from what the Prime Minister has just said-that the select committee of the house to be appointed and to which this measure will be referred, will be guided in its action by the same principles as guided previous committees in preparing the redistribution map, if I may so describe its work. In a word, the principles that have guided other committees have been, in the first instance, to follow as largely as possible the county municipal organizations in defining and delimiting the constituencies. The county municipal organization is that which is followed in municipal affairs and with respect to the judiciary and it is familiar to the people of the country generally. I suggest that it should again be adopted as largely as possible with respect to the defining of boundaries under the redistribution that is now to be made.
The second guiding principle is that the unit of representation in urban centres would necessarily be larger than that in rural constituencies. The reason for that is obvious. If it were not so, with the country as sparsely settled as it is in some parts, the rural constituencies would be difficult to control for purposes of administration. But there is a further and more important reason, and that is that as far as the urban constituencies are concerned, they have a means of voicing public opinion which rural constituencies have not. I need not mention the various organizations which exist in the urban centres, the large number of bodies such as boards of trade and commercial, industrial and social organizations.

Redistribution-Mr. Mackenzie King
all of which play a part in forming and expressing public opinion. But I would refer particularly to the effect of the press. The daily press of the country is for the most part, :f not exclusively, to be found only in urban centres. The rural press is, generally speaking, weekly, semi-weekly or bi-monthly, and the press from the cities finds its way into the country districts to a very great extent, whereas the same cannot be said to be true of the press of the rural parts. As hon. members well know there is no other single factor that so largely goes to influence public opinion as the press. What is done in that way is reflected again by what is said here on the part of hon. members.
There is a further reason also, which I think will be apparent and which will appeal to hon. members. It not infrequently happens that rural constituencies are represented in the House of Commons by gentlemen who reside in cities and urban municipalities, but the reverse, except in very rare instances, is not the case. It seldom happens that an urban constituency is represented by someone who resides the year round in a rural constituency, but there are in the house at the present time and have been in all previous parliaments many hon. members who have represented rural constituencies but who are more familiar with the life of the cities and the large towns than with the life and needs of the rural communities. The principle of a larger unit for urban representation has been accepted practically ever since confederation by committees which have dealt with this matter, and I hope and asume full recognition of it will be given by the committee to which this bill will be referred.
' There is an additional guiding principle, that, so far as reasonably can be arranged, there should1 be an effort at compactness in the shaping of constituencies. That permits of an expression of opinion from a community that is familiar with its own affairs, and in that way helps to give a more accurate representation of the views of the people./
Finally there is one other factor which I should mention, and that is that so far as it can be arranged there should be an equalization of the representation as between the different urban constituencies and as between the different rural constituencies; that is to say, as nearly as such can be worked out, having regard to the other guiding principles to which I have referred, there should be as between city constituencies a unit of representation approximating that in other cities, and as between rural constituencies there should also be as nearly as possible an equal unit of representation. Undoubtedly it would not be possible for a committee to work out any redistribution map with mathematical exactness. That cannot be expected. The most that can be expected is that the members of the committee will seek to be fair and just and to apply common sense in an effort to frame the redistribution map along the lines that I have indicated. The purpose of bringing together a number of members of the House of Commons around a common table to discuss with good intentions the framing of a redistribution that will be fair and equitable has been found to be an infinitely better method than the old one of having the government itself frame the map, in the first instance, and then bring it into this house for discussion. The report of the committee will of course be open to amendment, acceptance or rejection by the house, but it is to be hoped it will be so nearly a matter of general agreement, that none of these steps may be necessary.
May I point out that since this new method has been adopted of referring the question of delimiting the constituencies to a select committee of the house there has been unanimity on the part of the committee with respect to the measure that was subsequently recommended to the house. At all events agreement was arrived at. I think that was due to the fact that a real effort was made by the members of the redistribution committee to be as fair and just and use as much common sense as they could in framing the redistribution map. I believe that we shall be able to count on at least a like degree of agreement in any committee that may be appointed at this time.
May I add this further word? The Prime Minister has indicated that the committee is to be named forthwith. I assume that the proceedings of parliament will not continue much longer for the present, but it might be of advantage to those on the committee if its membership could be brought together before adjournment and the members themselves provided with what there may be available in the way of data, maps and the like, which later will have to be considered by the committee, and which if made available to the members at once would perhaps expedite the committee's work when it meets after the adjournment.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: May I call attention to the fact that we in the west, where there is any increase in population, have just as great a right to our proportion of the representatives that are due to us, and if we are going to begin to give fixed number of representatives to certain of the older provinces it is going to create a very serious situation across the west. There cannot be two or three different classes of Canadians in this country, with certain classes having superior rights to others. If a mistake -was made in giving a fixed number of representatives to Prince Edward Island there is no reason why we should follow a bad precedent. The way to get away from that is to amend the British North America Act so that Prince Edward Island would have only its due number and not a number out of proportion to the rest of the country.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
I agree with the last speaker (Mr. Woods-worth) that there should not be different classes of Canadians when it comes to representation in parliament. The right hon. the Prime Minister has accurately and fairly stated

to the house what the legal position is with regard to the basis of representation in the house.
I wish to call attention to an anomaly which is being discussed at the present to a considerable extent in my own province. As the right hon. gentleman has said, the basis of representation is the unit as determined by dividing the population of the province of Quebec by 65. The representation of the other provinces is supposed to be based on that unit of population. I think every hon. member of this house by a simple computation will see that the changes which are effected by one subsection of section 51 of the British North America Act work most unfairly in respect of the representation of the province of Quebec. I take the figures in bulletin No. 20 of the census of 1931, which show the quotient of the province of Quebec, of the new Quebec so far as its representation is concerned, to be 44,186. If you apply this quotient to Ontario you will find that if Ontario is granted 82 members, as it will be, and I agree that until a change is made in the British North America Act it should be done in that way, the unit in Ontario will be 41,849 as compared with 44,186 in the province of Quebec. Surely my friends from Ontario are just as well qualified as we are in the province of Quebec to represent the same number of people. But they will not, under the new redistribution; they will represent only a unit of 41,849 people. The anomaly of that situation is more glaring under the present redistribution because this great difference did not occur in 1921. In 1921, if the exception under subsection 4 of section 51 had not been applied, under the quotient Ontario would have had 80-86 members which would mean, under the act, 81 members. But this year the quotient of Ontario is not even 78, but 77-66. Therefore I say it is certainly unfair. I have tried to find in the debates on confederation and elsewhere the reason for the exception in subsection 4 of section 51, but have been unable to do so. This subsection is as follows:
On any such readjustment the number of members for a province shall not he reduced unless the proportion which the number of the population of the province bore to the number of the aggregate population of Canada at the then last preceding readjustment of the number of members for the province is ascertained at the then latest census to be diminished by one-twentieth part or upwards.
Why this provision? I cannot find why it appears; I should be pleased if some one could give me a reason. Perhaps it was inserted to help some of the smaller provinces, but when it works the way we see it will

Redistribution-Mr. Ralston
work this year, certainly it is an anomaly which works unfairly. I am sure hon. members from Ontario want only representation by population. Before confederation they fought for it, and that should be the principle governing that province. What amazes me is that this same principle is not working the other way. Why should not the representation decrease when its proportion of population with regard to the whole of Canada has not decreased by one-twentieth? Why should it increase if the number is increased by less than one-twentieth? As it is, any other province which would come under the same conditions keeps its representation, not on account of its own increase, but because of decreases in other parts of Canada,-and not of Quebec, which is taken as the pivot. If anybody can give me one sound reason for it, if anyone can tell me why Ontario should have only 41,000 as a unit of representation and w'e from Quebec should have 44,000, I am quite willing to listen, I cannot see how any reason could exist.
A suggestion was made that in order to equalize with Ontario, the number of representatives from Quebec should be increased. I do not think that would be a fair way of settling it. I believe the representation of *Quebec should remain at 65, as fixed by the British North America Act, but that subsection 4 of section 51 should disappear. Then we would have a real representation by population. The right hon. gentleman opposite has stated that before parliament meets again at the end of January there will be an interprovincial conference. There are certain changes in our constitution, and with regard to taxation, which seem desirable. I submit the Prime Minister should place this matter before the premiers from the various provinces. If that were done I believe they would come to the conclusion that subsection 4, which certainly works unfairly, ought to be repealed.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have observations to make on only two points in connection with this bill. First I should like to direct my remarks to the effect it will have on the province of Nova Scotia. I thoroughly agree with the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Cantley) that it gives us a very great feeling of regret, and even of sadness, to see a progressive reduction in representation from our province. He has pointed out, and I shall supplement his remarks with figures, that since 1881 there has been, after each decennial census, a reduction in representation. In 1881 we had 21
members; in 1891, 20; in 1901, 18; in 1911, 16; in 1921, 14, and this bill provides for only 12.
I realize the fact, namely that it is in the bond, and that technically, according to the interpretation of the British North America Act, we must bow to the inevitable and, at least for the purposes of this bill, accept the reduction being made. I do feel however that we should not allow this occasion to pass without recording the position of Nova Scotia, and the idea which the fathers of confederation had in mind at the time they adopted a certain principle of representation. I shall take only a moment to remind the house that at the conference the Hon. George Brown when introducing the resolution with regard to representation, intimated that the practical result would be that "while lower Canada certainly will not be less, and the lower provinces may increase in population, they cannot decrease in the number of representatives." In contradistinction to that I point out to the house the fact that at every decennial census there has been a decrease. I point out, further, that the fathers of confederation had adequate representation in mind, and not only the principle of representation by population.
In support of that let me cite the instances of the provinces which came into confederation after 1867. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) has been rather strong in his intimation that we must stick to the letter of the pact, and that the calculations must be made directly in accordance with the terms of the British North America Act. Let me remind him- and I do not do it in any spirit of criticism -that when Manitoba entered the confederation she had a representation amounting to less than the required unit for one member. Yet Manitoba was given a representation of four members. In 1881, I believe it was, a readjustment was made as had been provided in the act admitting Manitoba. At that time it was found that, under the strict arithmetical basis to which the hon. member has referred, Manitoba was entitled to only three members. The fact is however that when readjustment took place she was given five.
Let me remind the house further that when British Columbia entered confederation the strict principle was not applied. I need not be tender in my remarks because hon. members must realize that I am making these statements to the house simply to show that the arithmetical basis has not been the only principle upon which we have acted when fixing representations. When British Columbia entered confederation it had a total



Redistribution-Mr. Ralston
population of about 40,000 and was given representation of six members, and an irreducible minimum of six. Ten years after British Columbia entered she had only two units of representation, that is to say, her population entitled her to only two members. Ten years later, in 1891, she had a population which entitled her to only four members, if the unit of representation applicable to the maritime and other provinces which came into confederation originally, had been applied. Prince Edward Island had only five units of representation when she entered confederation, but was given six members. At the present time the representation of Prince Edward Island is four, the irreducible minimum. I just mention this to indicate to the house that it was not altogether arithmetic or mathematics that influenced those who were seeking to found and foster the Canadian idea of democratic institutions and representative government. So it is that Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island feel that they have made some contribution in men and women to the western provinces, the western provinces have had an increase not only in population but in territory as well, and we find ourselves today with the representation shifting to the west away from the provinces which originally entered confederation. I remind my friends that Nova Scotia was the cradle of representative institutions in British North America, and you cannot blame us for a feeling of regret and sadness that our representation is being reduced.
Let me close with this word taken from the case which was presented to the maritime commission three or four years ago.
There is surely something wrong with the system of representation which penalizes some provinces for the sacrifices they have made in sending their children and their means to upbuild the other parts of the dominion, and which would fail to make any special allowance in their representation in the Canadian parliament in respect of their isolated position which prevents them from enlarging their bounds out of the public lands of Canada.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, although it cannot be done in connection with this bill, that the suggestion of my hon. friend from Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe), might well be accepted by the right hon. Prime Minister, the matter might be made a subject of discussion at the inter-provincial conference, and in view of the fact that constantly during the last two or three sessions there has been forecast the possibility of amendments to the British North America Act, it seems to me this sub-
ject is one which might well engage the attention of those framing these amendments and discussing the subjects to be dealt with thereby.
So much for the general point. The other point is in connection with Nova Scotia, It is felt that there is grave doubt as to whether Nova Scotia during the last ten years has had its full representation. That comes about, as was pointed out to the commission on maritime claims, by reason of the fact that in calculating the unit of representation based on the 1921 census it seems there was included the portion of Quebec taken in under the legislation of 1898, with the result that the unit of representation was increased, with the consequence that, dividing that unit into the population of Nova Scotia the amount left over after the even number of members was found, was less than one half, whereas as a matter of fact had that addition to the population of Quebec not been included the amount left over would have been greater than one half-

Mr. Speaker, having been a member of the last redistribution committee, and having, I hope, taken my duties at that time somewhat seriously, I arrived at two or three opinions as a result of my experience which I should like to state briefly today. I am not going to comment on the general aspects of the bill, I think the procedure that has been followed the past years and which will be adopted is as fair and equitable as it very well can be. I think the bill we have, based as it is upon our constitution, the British North America Act, is the normal and proper bill on such an occasion, but there are one or two points which were the subject of very definite discussion the last time, which I have no doubt will be discussed just as strongly this coming year.
The first point was the general question of representation by population, "rep by pop" as it is popularly called; that is, the question of whether the rural and urban constituencies should have exactly the same unit of representation. In the last committee there was a very strong body of opinion in favour of "rep by pop," but there was a somewhat stronger body against it. I must say, Mr. Speaker, that I am absolutely in agreement with the position taken by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) in that respect; that is, that the rural constituencies should have a smaller unit of representation than the cities. After all, why do we have this representation? I assume that it is in

Redistribution-Mr. Speaknian
order that under our laws and our taxation customs absolute equality shall prevail throughout the country, so that each section of the population shall be dealt with fairly. But, as has been pointed out by the leader of the opposition, the representation in the House of Commons is not the only form of influence which has to do with the making of our laws or the formulation of our taxation policies. There are others. The right hon. gentleman referred to the question of the press, and undoubtedly in the matter of formulating and expressing public opinion the cities have a far greater opportunity through the public press than have the rural communities. But apart from that there is another question; the financial domination which is inseparable from the cities carries with it a tremendous influence which is not found in the rural communities. In that way, too, the cities have an opportunity to impress their beliefs, their ideas and their opinions upon the country and to put them into effect to a far greater extent than has a scattered rural population. Then there is the fact that through the centralization of population public opinion can be drawn together and expressed forcibly and adequately so much more easily and readily in the cities than is the case in the country.
For all these reasons I think it very essential that trie committee which will meet during the next part of this session should be very careful that the rural communities carry in every respect as fair a share as possible of influence upon the laws of the country. It must be recognized that from the very nature of our progressive civilization, making no reference to special laws which may favour the cities and which may naturally bring people together in industry, the proportion of our population found in the large centres must increase while the percentage found in the farming communities must decrease. There is no question about that. The fact that every new industry that is formed and every new want that comes into being is expressed in terms of industrial commodities makes it inevitable that this should be the case. On the other hand, however, there is no doubt that the rural portion of the community is of such tremendous importance that its viewpoint at all times must be adequately expressed.
As to the actual details of the bill, the Prime Minister has pointed to one or two factors which must be taken into consideration. First, of course, there is the factor of population, to ensure that after taking into

consideration the question of rural and urban constituencies, the population shall be as nearly as possible alike in the various constituencies. There is the question of natural boundaries which must be taken into account so far as possible. There is the question of accessibility, so that the lines of railways and highways shall be followed as nearly as possible. There is the question of community interest, to avoid as far as possible the division of community interests and to bring about their centralization. All those matters must be taken into account, but there is still another factor which appeared when the last bill was under consideration, and which undoubtedly will be found again. This is a factor which, to my mind, should be ignored as far as possible. I refer to the political factor. May I suggest that the members of the committee which is to be set up should avoid as far as possible this political factor, this desire which always has been found so to divide the ridings as to ensure a majority for one party or the other. I need only allude to that point and to glance at the faces of the older members of this house to assure myself that they understand the point. I think it very desirable that in this year of grace we should go a little beyond that and attempt so to carry on this redistribution that the people of the country, regardless of political affiliations, may have an equal chance to express their opinions when the time comes to do so. I only refer to that point because it is a question that is very dominant in the minds of the people at this moment. They are wondering today whether the committee will rise above those considerations or whether they will be influenced too much by them, as has been the case sometimes in the past.

Macdonald, who was then a minister of the crown from Nova Scotia, threshed out that matter very thoroughly. I am only speaking from what I understand to be the facts, since I was not in the house at that time, but my information is that allowance was made for the factor to which the hon. gentleman refers.
I understand that Mr. Macdonald pressed the matter very strongly but was overborne by mathematics and was unable to secure the retention of the additional membership to which the hon. gentleman has referred. I believe that on inquiry he will find this to be so, and I believe an investigation will satisfy the hon. gentleman that it is mathematically correct.
Further I should like to say that I do not think it probable that a provincial conference that has to deal with the problems with which we will have to deal will be in a position to discuss constitutional changes on general lines. The ex-Minister of Justice knows how contentious that subject is and how difficult of solution is the question of the amendment of the constitution on a large scale. That would involve a reconsideration of the question of the basis of representation in parliament. Sometimes I do think, and I believe most hon. members of the house will agree, that those who were responsible for the British North America Act were exceedingly wise men. When one thinks how, with changed conditions and new circumstances, we have been able to work out our problems within the elastic provisions of that statute, one has more and more regard, esteem and reverence for the genius of the men who prepared it, especially sections 91 and 92. When I look at section 51 I realize that those who had to deal with the problem felt that one day there would be a larger Canada and that sixty-five should be-I was very pleased to hear the hon. gentleman say that it was very proper that sixty-five was the unit-the unit. It is an amazing thing how the application of the principle mentioned in that section has kept pace with the expanding population of the country, the population of Quebec having kept pace and really more than kept pace with the growth of other parts of Canada. Of the older provinces, undoubtedly it was the province to select for a fixed
representation. The result is amazing when you contemplate it in the light of circumstances which have since transpired.
There is always a difficulty between the rural and urban populations.

I was rather amazed at the argument of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speak-man), who seemed fearful of political considerations prevailing in a committee which is to be selected by mathematical processes. The figures are very clear. We would have 11-265 members on the committee, the official opposition would have 7-265 and Labour, the Independents and the United Farmers of Alberta would have 1-469. They have less than one and one-half and they are being given two, while the Liberals and Conservatives are losing their half. It was a rather strange argument which the hon. member used. He made a plea for the recognition of the rural population through a higher ratio of representation in the house than that enjoyed by the urban population. It rather negatives the argument of the hon. member for Queuec East (Mr. Lapointe), it was an assertion that 50,000 people in one part of Canada should have but one member while
Redistribution-Mr. Bennett

If he was fearful of political considerations prevailing and felt that there should be equality in every part of Canada with regard to representation, how is his first plea' supported? What he did in the early part of his argument was to contend that one man residing in the country should have as much influence as two and three residing in the city. He then closed by saying that political considerations should not prevail in order that the farmer would have the same rights as the city man and be in the same position. I leave it at that.
I desire to associate myself with what has been said in comparing the present method of proceeding by way of committee and that taken by the old parliaments when they themselves made the redistribution. In the old days, the government of the day brought in its bill, which was sometimes called a jerrymander bill.

I had not intended to go into this matter very deeply, Mr. Speaker, but as I said at the outset of my remarks, it is never very safe to make too definite statements, especially if you are in public life, or too definite promises as to what you may do in the future, and when I say that I am not referring to the promises made by the Prime Minister in regard to unemployment. I am referring to the slogan, if you like to call it that, which the Prime Minister nailed to the mast during his campaign. In connection with the railways he said, "Amalgamation never; competition ever." I believe that before very long the Prime Minister will have to reverse that slogan, because if we continue as we are going at present in connection with the two railways, with the consequent waste, this country will not be able to bear the burden.
I am out of order, perhaps, but I should like to make just a reference to the recommendations made by the royal commission. They advocate compulsory cooperation. This may be the only thing that can be done, but I will say that I have no great faith in compulsory cooperation; the two things just do not go together. I say further that in the future we will find the old slogan "competition is the life of trade" out of date; in certain respects at least competition is the death of trade and of prosperity. I hope that in future the slogan of Canadians and of the world will be cooperation rather than competition.
The question now is how far we can go in the direction of these socialistic tendencies, if you like to so call them. I am not prepared to say. It has been suggested that we should have a national bank, and that may be a good suggestion. It has been suggested also, and I am rather inclined to favour the suggestion, that we should at least mutualize our life insurance companies, and there may be many other directions in which we might proceed. The point I want to make, however, is that fMr. Euler.]
I believe some modification of our present system is necessary. We may survive the present difficulties; after a while we may turn that mythical corner of which we have heard so much, around which we will find prosperity. I do not desire to be pessimistic, but I am a little afraid it may be some time before we turn that corner. Whether or not that is so, however, some time later we will have another period of depression, and that will happen again and again unless we modify our system.
Some people think depressions are absolutely necessary under our capitalistic system. I do not believe that, but if it be so, then so much the worse for our system. In the olden days people believed that epidemics of smallpox, yellow fever and other diseases were dispensations of Providence, but science has overcome those epidemics. It does seem to me that it should not be regarded as inevitable that these alternate periods of depression and prosperity should exist in a country such as Canada. I feel that whether or not we see the way clear, at least we should make some effort to find a remedy. If there is one thing in the public mind at this time-and this applies not only to the people who have not very much by way of money or possessions but also to every member of this house, as it applies to myself- it is the constant fear of the future. We do not know what the future will bring, yet we are living in a country and in a world that can and should produce enough for everyone if that production is properly distributed. Surely there must be men of ability in this country, men of good will if you like, men like those who accomplished wonders during the development of the world's civilization, who can find a remedy, so that we should not regard ourselves as impotent to make further advances in the direction we desire to go.

Mr. Speaker, in connection with this motion I shall detain the house but a few moments in dealing with the conditions which prevail in the country generally and in connection with the fishing industry in particular, which industry has been hit as hard as any natural industry which could be mentioned.
Taking the conditions in the country as a whole, I think we are all agreed that they are perhaps worse than any which have prevailed at any time since confederation. There can be no division of opinion in connection with a situation where between seven and eight hundred thousand people are receiving relief. While we may say that it should not be so and while we do say that promises were made that it would be otherwise, for the moment we must devote ourselves to endeavouring to find some solution for the problem and some mitigation for the conditions which will exist this winter.
There is going to be a day, perhaps not far distant, when an accounting will be demanded of the stewardship of those who are in power at the present time. There is going to be a day when men will ask a reason for the disastrous condition which has followed the very flagrant breaches of undertakings which were given in 1930. But we can afford for the moment to leave that to one side in order to discuss conditions as they exist at the present time and any thing which may be done to ameliorate them. The other evening the Prime Minister made a statement which was regarded in the country as being rather important, namely, that a provincial conference was being called, but with due respect- and I am not making this criticism in any carping spirit-I felt that perhaps too much emphasis was laid by him on matters that are not essential at this time. It was pointed out to us that this conference would be held

Fishing Industry-Mr. Ralston
in order to discuss amendments to the Companies Act. Of course such amendments are important, but they pale into insignificance beside the question of unemployment and that of the necessity of our people having an opportunity to earn a living. Amendments to the Insurance Act and the question of provincial and federal jurisdiction were to be discussed as well. The matter of spheres of taxation was also to be taken up. I felt that the real object for which this conference ought to be called was somewhat beclouded by the extended references which the Prime Minister made to those matters which would be discussed at a provincial conference at any time, iD any year in the history of the dominion and that the real object for which this conference should be called, and I hope the real one which the Prime Minister has in mind, was the discussion of unemployment and relief conditions and the possibility of providing an opportunity for our people to work.
The right hon. leader of the government (Mr. Bennett) has repeatedly in the house mentioned the constitutional question. I do not think there is any difference of opinion in this chamber or in the country with regard to the constitution. We all agree that in times of national emergency the dominion has jurisdiction to legislate or to impose its will upon the people of the provinces; that it assumes paramount legislative jurisdiction. But we are not at this time-and I commend this to my right hon. friend-talking about the question of imposing obligations on provinces or on the people of the provinces; we are talking about the possibility of conferring some benefit upon them and there is in the British North America Act, that sacred ark of the covenant, nothing which prevents us from doing so. My right hon. friend draws a distinction between a national emergency and a national condition. The people do not care one whit whether it is a national emergency or a national condition; they are hungry and cold and need shelter.
They are in distress.

Yes, they are in distress. It does not make any difference what you call it, if the federal authority has power within itself to deal with the situation, it seems to me that my right hon. friend cannot get rid of the responsibility. All the discussion that there has been about the British North America Act, the jurisdiction of the provinces and the inviolate field which must be maintained there with regard to legislation amounts to little when we have the responsibility definitely assumed by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon). He has made the
position of the government abundantly clearr as a minister of the crown in a federal government which takes its jurisdiction from the British North America Act, he says this: "No one need worry about being adequately supplied with food, clothing, fuel and shelter." There is a responsibility assumed, and I do not think there is any need of a lengthy discussion on the question of the constitution. The government has assumed the obligation and the question is now: What is the best way to carry it out? I say frankly to my right hon. friend that when you use federal money, for instance, as it is used in connection with the Old Age Pensions Act, you may impose conditions and say to the people: You may use this money only provided those conditions are observed. My right hon. friend two years ago, in bringing down the provision for unemployment relief, expressly imposed by order in council provisions in regard to accounts, and in regard to supervision. All those were put into the order in council and nobody suggested that this was unconstitutional. So in the same way we can suggest and impose conditions whenever we pay money out of the federal treasury. Nobody doubts that the Dominion of Canada has power to pay money out of the federal treasury for these purposes of relief. The Minister of Labour has admitted that and the question of jurisdiction is rather beyond the point now, having regard to the serious situation which confronts us.
I do not intend at any length to go into the question of the method whereby that general principle is to be carried out. I say this to my right hon. friend, since he has suggested that a provincial conference should be held. I reiterate what my right hon. leader has said so frequently that the people of Canada are entitled to see some mobilization of the business, industrial, agricultural and economic forces of this dominion in order that plans may be worked out to deal with this situation. I do not think that is a reflection on the government. The same thing is being done in the country to the south of us. It seems to me that the problem is far and away beyond one simply of government and administration, and while the government have the responsibility for the expenditure of this money, at the same time I do not think they would be humiliating themselves in the slightest if they took the advice of some national council which could survey the field broadly, not from the point of view of legislative jurisdiction alone. What I mean by that is this: I mean there may be in the dominion certain industries which, if assisted to a reasonable extent by a direct grant of money, if you like, might provide substantial

Fishing Industry-Mr. Ralston
employment. For instance, those who are engaged in and familiar with the lumbering industry might be able usefully to advise the government in that respect. With regard to plans which might be made as to conditions under which the money is to be spent, people throughout the dominion could give advice out of their ripe experience and their knowledge of the business in which they are engaged and the part of the country from which they come. That is not handing jurisdiction over to a federal commission or a violation of the British North America Act, but it is carrying out the idea of national cooperation and the mobilization of national forces. That is what has been suggested repeatedly and what is at last being adopted in a more or less modified form by my right hon. friend when he suggests conferences. Let me point out to him that this matter of conferences is not new. He had in 1930 exactly the idea which I am now trying to express. I find in his speech on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, he complains on February 24, 1930, about conditions in Canada being very, very bad. I quote from page 18 of Hansard of that date where he is reported as saying: What about conditions in this dominion at this moment? What about conditions from east to west? It is true that part of the unemployment is seasonal; but since the beginning of the year I have traversed Canada from Victoria to the far east and in every city of this dominion, east and west, there is abnormal unemployment, so that men who are accustomed to give, as I have been, to assist those who are unable to earn sufficient to keep body and soul together, have never before seen such distress as I have seen in the communities I have visited.
Then he goes on:
What was the Minister of Labour doing? What was the Prime Minister doing? Were they calling conferences? The only conferences they were calling were conferences to determine how best they could ward off the blows of an indignant people. The only conferences they were having were as to how they might increase their power and retain their positions. I have received a telegram from the secretary or the Miners' Union at Fernie indicating that their mine is closed because it is owmed in the Unitec, states by one of the great railway systems and in pursuance of the policy of Mr. Hoover to give employment to the people in that country they are going to mine coal in the Lnited States and shut down the Canadian mine. What is the Minister of Labour doing about the matter ? Where was there a conference of Canadian business men?
This is what we are suggesting.
Were they asked to meet together? They were not.

When a meeting was called by Mayor Webb m W innipeg of all the mayors of western towns and representatives of western provinces as well, the minister will recall that he was to attend and it was given out that he was ill and unable to go, but his illness was not so great as to prevent him from attending banquets around but not on that particular date.
There was a clear intimation by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister that he did believe in the calling of conferences, the calling of those who had experience in connection with the general business and industrial life of the country. The seriousness of the condition then did not compare with conditions today, and I submit to him, even though two years have passed, and although the delay has been very harmful, it is not too late for some such conference as this to be called in order that this country, if it is going to revive from the situation in which it finds itself, may have the assistance of the brains and experience of our business leaders and of those engaged in both natural and manufacturing industry all over this country. That has got to be done, and I submit to my right hon. friend that that should be done now regardless of whether or not an interprovincial conference is going to be called. I mention this in passing because I do feel that we should not spare any endeavour to impress on my right hon. friend the necessity for national organization to take hold of the situation in which the country finds itself at the present time.
I want to refer for a moment or two to an industiy that has not been mentioned here. Agriculture has been mentioned, and there has been a good deal of talk about manufacturing. I want to refer to the fishing industry in which are engaged in the province of Nova Scotia some 20,000 men, and which industry provides, or should provide, a livelihood for these men and their families.
An interesting sidelight came to me recently in connection with this matter of fish. We are all looking for markets for lumber, for wheat, copper and fish. I pick up the St. John Telegraph-Journal of November 23, and I find there the menu provided at the penitentiary of St. Vincent de Paul for a week. Do you know I have searched that from start to finish, and there is not a single item of fish on the menu.

I beat you to it. I drew
the matter to the attention of the Fisheries Association.

Fishing Industry-Mr. Ralston
My hon. friend is always ahead. I only want to say to the government, no wonder these men in St. Vincent de Paul rebel.

They may refuse fish, just as
they have refused porridge.

If you put fish on the
menu I think probably those men would return to sanity and be perfectly tractable.
I commend that suggestion to the minister, not to the Fisheries Association, but to the Minister of Justice whose department provides the menu in St. Vincent de Paul. That is an instance of what goes on. Even for Friday I cannot find fish on the menu.
Let me speak for a moment with regard to conditions in the fishing industry as I know them in the western end of Nova Scotia. These men and women are not asking for sympathy or relief if they can have an opportunity to earn a living in their vocation.
I want to point out to the government that there is a possibility of at least substantially improving the situation down there without going to the extent of relief; that is, the payment of actual dollars which would otherwise be necessary. I want to give two or three instances to the house showing what these men earn who are engaged in this hazardous industry.
Let me remind the house that the individual shore fisherman and the men who go out in a two-man or three-man boat probably out at three in the morning and do not return till late in the afternoon. He may have had a poor day or a fairly good day. He has to pay for his oil and his gasoline and his bait and for the upkeep of his boat, and sometimes he does not catch enough fish to pay his expenses at the very low prices for fish now prevailing. I have here some actual examples of what these fishermen have earned, men who have persistently pursued their vocation in an endeavour to make a living.
Here is one case of two men going out two months day after day and getting a total of $64 for the two months' work. Interest, upkeep and depreciation comes to $20 for a boat probably costing $600. The net result is $44 for two months' work, on which these men have to keep themselves and their wives and families.
Here is another case of two men going out day after day, and at the end of the trip they average $15 for two months' work. They get $36 altogether. Their out-of-pocket expenses were $21, leaving $15 or $7.50 apiece for the two months.

Here is another case of men going out in a schooner for a trip of eight weeks. I find that these men got a little o"ver $25 per man for that eight weeks' period.
Here is the case of two men making eleven trips covering a two months' period, going cut in a two-man boat, and making $92 altogether; out-of-pocket expenses $38; $20 for interest, upkeep and depreciation; leaving $34 to divide between himself and his buddy. Think of it, $34 for two months' work for two men.
Here is another fisherman whose gross is $56; out-of-pocket expenses $26; $20 for interest, upkeep and depreciation; actual net, $10 to be divided between two men for two months' work.
Another fisherman gets $26 in a two-months' period; expenses $16, leaving him $10, out of which he has to pay interest, upkeep and depreciation.
Here is the case of a three-man boat making ten trips, with a gross of $138; interest, upkeep and depreciation, $48; leaving $90 to be divided among three men for two months' work.
Another instance. A four-man boat makes seven trips and grosses $123.15; out-of-pocket expenses $63; interest, upkeep and depreciation $40, leaving S20 to be divided amongst four men for two months' work.
The house might ask why is there this difference between the number of trips that these men take. The difference is due to this: Men who are away behind cannot afford to go out except on the very best days. They cannot afford to pay for gasoline and oil and bait and run the risk of a bad trip and a nonproductive catch. I emphasize again that this is hazardous work. It is the hardest sort of work, and these men are constantly at it in an endeavour to make a living.
You ask me, what is the remedy? The situation is this. That fish is bringing from three-quarters of a cent to one cent a pound. The difficulty is that these men are directly in competition with the trawlers which have been repeatedly mentioned in this house and in orders in council and even in statutes. I submit that at this time the remedy is for the government either definitely to refuse licences for the trawlers which are operating or to so reduce the number of trawlers, so that the fisherman will have the first chance at the market. I am not going into the history of the trawler situation except to put clearly on record that the Maritime Fisheries Commission in 1928 made a report, the majority recommending the absolute abolition of the trawler, and the minority, the chairman.
