Fishing Industry-Mr. Ralston
recommending that the trawlers be reduced at least to an extent that would give the fishermen the first opportunity at the market. The government of that day made an investigation into the whole matter, and after the fullest inquiry by the Minister of Fisheries massed an order in council whereby it was prodded that the trawlers should be licensed ind that the licence fee should amount to one cent a pound for non-Canadian-built rawlers, and three-quarters of a cent a pound for fish landed from Canadian trawlers, and that after April 1, 1932, only Canadian-built trawlers should operate. The tax was imposed. Trawler interests were very much against it. It was paid by some companies and refused by others. Action was brought, with the result that the order in council was held to be ultra vires, that is to say beyond the scope of the act under which it was passed. That was after the present government came into power but no action was taken to reinstate the order in council or to make it effective by legislation, although that could have been done. But the present government, following a considered policy, passed an order in council under the act whereby it was provided that two things should take place, first that trawlers should be licensed and secondly-a more or less important provision-that trawlers should be marked so that they could easily be identified in case of the destruction of fishermen's gear. But, this proviso was put in-and it is to this proviso that I refer the government-that trawlers should be licensed only to the extent that was necessary to make up for any deficiency in the supply of fish from shore fishermen. That brings me to my point. I submit the time has arrived when snore fishermen can supply every pound of fish required. Trawlers are landing vast quantities with the result that the fishermen can only dispose of about 25 per cent of normal production. If shore fishermen were given an opportunity to supply the market the price of fish to them would show a substantial increase, and they would have an opportunity to make, perhaps not an adequate living, but at least some further earnings.
My plea to this government at the present time is to take the steps which, under the order in council they can take to stop the operation of the trawler, so long at least as the shore fishermen are able to supply the demand. I say to hon. members opposite from the information I have received there is plenty of reason to believe that the shore fishermen could supply the demand now obtaining. I do not wish to labour the point, but I submit I have placed before the

government something in the nature of concrete action it should take. I have placed before it something definite which can be done. My hon. friends may consider this something in the nature of a relief measure needed at the present time. Not only would it be a relief measure, but it would be a measure of justice which should be extended under the order in council of this government. If they were to take the action I have suggested they would do much toward relieving the situation in fishing communities.
I repeat my statement of last year, that fishing communities do not want assistance if they can be allowed to work out their own destiny. They would rather work and pay their own way through the natural resources at their disposal, than take a dole, charity or assistance. The present situation is that if something is not done for them their only alternative is to ask the Minister of Labour through the provincial government to do something by way of relief. I say the best relief which can be given to the fishermen of the maritime provinces is an opportunity to help themselves and to enjoy the markets there for them, provided they are given an opportunity to free themselves from the competition of trawlers which, after all, under the legislation now on the statute books, and by the order in council, are only auxiliary to the shore fishermen. Our market is supposed, primarily, to be given to those fishermen.
The general problem of unemployment has been fully covered, and at this time I urge upon the government particularly this one matter, namely the reconsideration of the trawler situation, so that there may be a wiping out of or substantial curtailment in the operation of trawlers. Such change should obtain until the fishermen are able to take up the slack in the market and are able to enjoy to the full the market which, in fact, is really theirs. There can be no question about the foresight, ability or enterprise of our fishermen. All they want is an opportunity on the market free from trawler competition which even hon. members on the government side of the house admit, should be used only for the purpose of implementing the supply in case that supply cannot be filled from other sources.
I am informed that the shore fishermen could supply the present demand, and that the price is very low. If regulations were enforced against the trawlers, no doubt the price would be substantially improved. I urge upon the government in the strongest possible manner the reconsideration of this matter.

Fruit Growing-Mr. W. A. Fraser

Mr. Speaker, I should like to take only a few moments of the time of the house concerning a matter affecting the fruit growers of the province of Ontario. My remarks at this time arise from a question I asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce a few days ago in connection with the export to Great Britain of a cargo of canned fruit and vegetables shipped by Canadian Canners from St. Catharines, Ontario. My question was as follows:
May I ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce whether about one-third of a cargo of canned fruit loaded at St. Catharines on a Norwegian tramp was shipped from Medina, New York, and labelled with Canadian Canners labels, to be conveyed by that steamer to the British market.
The reply of the minister on the following day is as follows:
Yesterday the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Fraser), under the guise of a question, made a statement as follows, that:
About one-third of a cargo of canned fruit loaded at St. Catharines on a Norwegian tramp was shipped from Medina, New York, and labelled with Canadian Canners labels, to be conveyed by that steamer to the British market.
In the first place, I wish to say that a statement of that kind, unchallenged and unrefuted, would certainly do serious damage to Canadian trade. I therefore made immediate and very careful inquiries and am able to inform the house that there is not a word of truth in the statement. The goods so canned were the product of Canadian farms, fruit and vegetables, and canned in the factories of Canadian canneries under the inspection and supervision of the inspectors of the Department of Agriculture in accordance with Canned Foods and Meats Act. In every sense this was a Canadian shipment, and I add this, that far from permitting the impression to go abroad that in any way Canada was not playing the game in its trade with the United Kingdom, the fact is that Canada has every reason to be proud both of the magnitude of the shipment and of its contents.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make this statement: I am very deeply interested not only in the fruit growing industry, but in the canning industry of Ontario, and I would be the last member in the house who would wish in any way to damage their interests. This time however I am not going to ask a question, but I am going to make a statement, or several statements, which I am prepared to substantiate.
Before proceeding I should like to commend and congratulate the representatives of the fruit branch in Canada, and in the old country, for the splendid work they have done in the interests of fruit growers and canners. Let
me go farther, and congratulate the government, inasmuch as I believe that some of the clauses in the agreement with Great Britain which pertain to apples will prove, and are proving, beneficial to the apple growers and the canning industry of the province of Ontario. Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, I have this objection to make concerning the remarks of the Minister of Trade and Commerce in reply to my question. I still maintain I asked a question; I placed before the minister a question asking for information, and based upon the fact that complaints had been lodged with representatives of certain departments in the city of Ottawa that the Canadian Canners are importing, and have been importing pears and other fruits from New York state, paying the duty of two cents per pound, canning them in Canada- as the minister has truly said-under the inspection of the Department of Agriculture, yet, nevertheless canning American or New York state pears and peaches in Canadian canneries, taking advantage of the rebate of 99 per cent and the duty of two cents per pound, and shipping them to the old country market as Canadian products. Now, Mr. Speaker, I make that statement because I believe it is in the interests of the fruit growers, that every hon. member should realize that this practice is being carried on, that the canners of this country are taking advantage of the low price this year of pears in New York state, $10 a ton to be exact, paying the 2 cents a pound duty, securing the rebate, and thus hammering down the price to the fruit growers in western Ontario. That is the point that was behind my question addressed to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I submit that in view of the facts that I am giving to the house-and I can prove what I say-the minister should have considered my question as that of one seeking information, and, in view of the publicity the matter has had through the press of Ontario, he should have been a little more careful about insinuating a lack of interest in the fruit grower.
Now, Mr. Speaker, just one word more. In the interests of the fruit growers and pear producers of western Ontario, regardless of the statements reported in the press as having been made by officials of the Ontario and federal governments and of Canadian canners in connection with this shipment on the Norwegian tramp that I referred to, may I suggest that this government take steps to prevent the fruit growers of Ontario being subject by reason of the drawback to the unfair competition of the extremely low prices

Fruit Growing-Mr. Stevens
existing through over-production in New York state and exporting fruit grown there as a Canadian product. That I submit for the consideration of the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce and his colleagues.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. H. STEVENS (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext: I feel it is necessary for me to reply to the further statement made by the hon. member. The hon. member has stated clearly today that he charges that Canadian Canners have been importing foreign pears and shipping them to the United Kingdom, to which hon. members sitting around him cried "shame."

Always done for years,
under the Liberal government.
His further statement is that Canadian Canners have used this condition for the hammering down of prices to the Ontario growers.
The hon. gentleman quibbled about it the other day.
The statement is untrue.

I did not quibble. The only reason I referred to this the other day and the only reason I refer to it again is this, that whether the hon. gentleman realizes it or not, the language in which he couched his alleged question and the language which he used today is in my opinion calculated to damage Canadian trade with Great Britain, and I think it necessary and desirable that it should be cleared up very definitely. I made careful inquiries into this matter, as I stated, and I have made further inquiries since, and I am advised-and later I will have exact figures to support this-that a comparatively small proportion of the shipment made from Hamilton the other day was composed of canned goods the contents of which were foreign to Canada.
Oh, oh.

Wait a moment. It has been the practice of the canners in western Ontario and other parts, but chiefly western Ontario, for many years, after the season is over for canning Canadian fruit, to import large quantities of grapefruit, pineapples, and other fruits for canning purposes, thus keeping the canning factories going. No one can have any criticism of that. In addition, it has been the practice of canners in western Ontario to import considerable quantities of pears for canning in Canada, to which no objection can be taken. There is nothing sinister about it, nothing wrong about it, it is a perfectly 
legitimate trade. But it happens that a very small quantity, I am told, if any, found its way into this particular large export shipment to which reference has been made.
That is at least some admission.

Another point the hon. gentleman has raised is the question of hammering down prices. I have been supplied with information regarding prices paid, as follows:
We paid Canadian fruit growers this year $40 a ton for Bartlett pears, $40 a ton for peaches, and about $12 a ton for apples. In the western states, from which our chief competition in the British and foreign markets comes, the growers received only $10 a ton for No. 1 pears. $0 a ton for No. 2 pears and $2.50 a ton for apples. New York state prices for Bartlett pears were $20 a ton and $10 a ton for Keefer pears.
Now this will indicate the competition that Canadian canners are confronted with in regard to the packing of goods for the export market. As I have already stated, the company assures me very definitely that this shipment contained but a very small proportion of this fruit.

What
proportion?

In addition to that the
practice in Canada has been in some cases to import considerable quantities of apples for the purpose of making pectin, which is used in Canada by jam manufacturers and those who put up various preserved fruits, to be added in the packing of these fruits and the manufacture of these jams as a jellying ingredient. It is also exported. This is a fruit ingredient which is quite legitimate and proper and good trade, and there is nothing about it that is in any sense to be criticized. I think, sir, that it is only fair to this company, particularly in view of the cries of hon. gentlemen a moment ago of "shame," when the hon. member was making his statement, it is only fair to a Canadian company that is trying to do business with countries outside of Canada, whether in the empire or out of it, that we should give them a bit of commendation for their efforts in promoting this foreign trade. I deplore more than I oan say any suggestions from influential members on the floor of this 'house regarding t'he practices followed by this and other Canadian companies.
Will the hon. minister permit a question?

Surely.

Fruit Growing-Mr. Gray

For my
own information I would like to be quite clear on this point: Is the house to understand that canners may bring in, under the conditions that I have mentioned a few minutes ago, American or foreign pears and ship them under the economic trade agreements and take advantage of the British preference, provided they are canned in this country?

It is as clear as day under the law. I will explain as well as I can, subject to not having precise percentages before me and therefore being unable to speak with entire accuracy. Goods manufactured in Canada have access to the British market under the preference if they carry the percentage of Canadian content prescribed by the British regulations. Just what that percentage is in regard to canned fruits I cannot at the moment tell my hon. friend, but I can secure the information. I suggest this however, speaking merely from my own opinion, that it is altogether probable that the value of, say, raw pears, we will take them as an illustration, as compared with the value of the completed article, including the cans, the packing, the shipping and so on, would be in such proportion as to meet that requirement. I expect that it would, and if it does-I will put the "if" in there-is it not legitimate that they should be so shipped?

Mr. Speaker, on this important matter I do not propose to allow the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) again to think he has given this house the last word. On November 23 the minister gave the house what he intended to be the last word with respect to this matter, which was brought up by my hon. friend from Northumberland (Mr. Fraser) who was not in the house at the time and who, at the earliest possible moment, brought to the attention of the house the true facts. Let me read again the reply as given by the minister on Wednesday of this week:
Yesterday the hon. member for Northumberland Qlr. Fraser), under the guise of a question, made a statement as follows. . . .
Any hon. member reading the question of the hon. member for Northumberland will realize that it has not even the suggestion of being a statement; it was a straight question asked of the minister by a member of this house. The minister went on:
In the first place, I wish to say that a statement of that kind, unchallenged and unrefuted, would certainly do serious damage to Canadian trade. I therefore made immediate and very careful inquiries . . .
The minister made immediate and careful inquiries and gave the house what he found as a result.
. . . and am able to inform the house that there is not a word of truth in the statement.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce, representing the trade of Canada, rises in his place and tells the hon. member for Northumberland that he was not telling the truth when he said that a portion of the goods were brought in from New York state, canned here and sent out under the guise of Canadian canned products. Now the minister has turned around; he says that some part of the shipment was brought in from New York state. He does not give the proportion; he leaves the impression that it was a very small part. Let me continue:
The goods so canned were the product of Canadian farms . . .
May I ask the minister if that was correct?
Absolutely.

They were the product of New' York state farms, brought in here and canned and sent to the United Kingdom under the guise of Canadian fruit. The British have already stated that they will not allow our wheat to proceed through United States ports except under a through label, and I ask the minister if he expects the British to say we are playing the game when we bring in New York pears, can them in Canadian factories and ship them out as the product of Canadian farms.
Talking nonsense.

Talking nonsense? The minister was talking nonsense not only today but on Wednesday as well, w'hen he said there was not a word of truth in the statement made by the hon. member for Northumberland. Let me tell my hon. friend that lie has not brought much credit on the Department of Trade and Commerce, over which he presides.
At one o'clock the house took recess.
The house resumed at three o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at one o'clock we were discussing a matter covered by a question asked by the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Fraser), a few days ago. I must say that we have listened to the tears which have rolled and fallen from the eyes of certain hon. members regarding the fruit business-

How do you listen to tears?

Fruit Growing-Mr. Chaplin

You could almost hear
them, they fell in a stream. These hon. gentlemen become interested in fruit only when they are in opposition. I should like to refer for a moment to the actions taken by hon. members opposite in connection with rebates. From their remarks one would think that rebates came into effect only recently whereas this legislation has been on the statute books for a considerable time. Why did they not object to it before? I have sat on both sides of the house, I have objected to certain rebates, but not one hon. member opposite would support me. The system is wrong, but hon. members opposite did not attempt to correct it.
The question asked by the hon. member for Northumberland was as follows:
May I ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce whether about one-third of a cargo of canned fruit loaded at St. Catharines on a Norwegian tramp was shipped from Medina, New York, and labelled with Canadian Canners labels, to be conveyed by that steamer to the British market.
What does the house think of a question like that? That is simply making a statement; the hon. gentleman either knew or did not know that that stuff came from New York. In fact, it never came from Medina.

should like to ask the hon. member how many Bartlett pears or peaches are grown in his riding?

Not one. I answer the

Read the agreement; it states, "grown, produced or manufactured in Canada."

"Grown, produced or
manufactured in Canada." Does not this come under the heading of manufactured in Canada? While the hon. member is attempting to divert me from this subject, I should like to ask him: If these rebates were not allowed, how could the country export anything in the way of rubber, silk or cotton goods? Hypocrisy.

Let me tell the hon. member something about hypocrisy in connection with his own actions. He knows that under the Liberal regime the department which had charge of customs permitted the duty paid on automobile parts coming into the country to be considered as part of the Canadian content.
That has nothing to do with these empire trade agreements.

Who said anything about rebates now? Under the British arrangement any goods which can qualify as -being of fifty, and sometimes sixty per cent Canadian content, are considered as products of this country. Many goods come in from the old country which are not more than fifty per cent English, and yet they are allowed to come in under the agreement.
Fruit is allowed to come into Canada after paying a duty and the Canadian Canners are allowed under the law to obtain a rebate when such goods are exported. This is exactly the same system as applies to other manufacturers; no more consideration is given

Fruit Growing-Mr. Malcolm
to the fruit canners than is given to the manufacturers of other products. In spite of these facts, hon. members have tried to make it appear as though the farmers of this country were being injured.
May I ask the hon. member a question?
Sit down a minute; the hon. member had his say and he will not answer any questions asked of him.
The hon. member for West Lambton was permitted to -make his speech without interruption from any part of the nouse.
I merely asked the hon. member if I could ask him a question. He has refused and I am sitting down.

It is out of order to interrupt a speaker in this way. When a member speaking is asked whether or not he will permit a question, he signifies his willingness to be interrupted by taking his seat; when he does not do so he indicates that he does not wish to be interrupted.
The facts are that this fruit was packed in Canada, the cans were made in Canada and certain work was done in Canada. In some instances fruit was allowed to come in.
Trucked in.
No, not trucked in either. The hon. member is very free with interruptions. He is talking about something of which he knows nothing, and usually people talk the loudest when they know the least.
That is hardly in order either.

The fruit business is of a seasonal nature. Take peaches, for example. This fruit is on the market for only five or six weeks, and the same thing applies to Bartlett pears. What did the present government do?
What did the Minister of Trade and Commerce do?

Will the hon. member try to be quiet just for once? This is the same old calf story.
The fruit business is seasonal. The fruit is available only in its ripened state; it cannot be kept even in cold storage for more than a week or two. When the season is over, no more fruit is available. In order to protect the fruit farmers of this country during the season, this government has put an embargo upon fruit coming in from the United States.
The previous government promised to do this, but they did not. When the former Minister of Finance, Mr. Dunning, introduced his budget he told the house that it was impossible to put a seasonal tariff upon fruit. Six days afterwards he did introduce a seasonal tariff but it proved to be unworkable. This government has a tariff which is workable. Fruit is allowed to enter the country only after our own fruit has gone off the market; the embargo is not lifted until the ripened fruit season is over. The Canadian canners pay twice as much for Canadian fruit as they would have to pay for American fruit, but they are not permitted to buy American fruit while our own is on the market. That is something the opposition never did for the farmer and never would do. Heaven knows we asked them often enough to do it.
I have no interest in this matter; I am not interested in any canning company, but I hate to see men get up in this house and talk until the cows come home upon a subject about which they know nothing. That has happened on more than one occasion. I come from a county where there are over twenty-five canning factories; the fruit industry of Lincoln county is as large as if not larger than that in any other county in Canada. I know something of conditions there, and something of conditions in the trade, and when one sees members get up and talk in this fashion it is absolutely sickening.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin) has certainly made a few facts abundantly clear. He spoke quite correctly with respect to the fact that Canada's export trade in manufactured products was not confined entirely to the production and further processing of Canadian goods and that much of our export trade was built up on raw materials which came from other parts of the empire and other parts of the world. He mentioned the rubber industry. It is true we enjoy within the British Empire considerable export trade in rubber products, the cotton of course, coming from either Egypt or the United States and the rubber from Malaysia. We enjoy a considerable market in other countries for canned fruits and vegetables and in the past, in order to have continuity of operation of our canneries, as the hon. member for Lincoln has said, we have permitted the importation of fruits and vegetables for canning in Canadian factories. I do not think anyone in the house disagrees in general with the principle of trying to have continuity of work in an industry where the Canadian product is seasonal, nor
Fruit Growing-Mr. Malcolm

do I think anyone objects particularly to the importation of fruits which are not grown in Canada, such as grapefruit, oranges and fruits of that type. This at least gives the Canadian workman an occupation during a season of the year when the Canadian product is not available for canning. I think, however, the hon. member for Lincoln was wrong in regard to his statement on embargoes. I do not think there has ever been an embargo placed on fruit for canning purposes. I may be mistaken.
The hon. member is mistaken. I know there has been.

Well, I was of that
opinion, and I stand corrected if the hon. member is quite sure of the fact.
I know it.

But there is another
point to which I should like to make slight reference. We have made some agreements with the British Empire and it has been heralded, I think rather broadly across this continent, that by these agreements the Canadian producers are to benefit. The Canadian producers will benefit in many instances; they certainly will benefit on raw fruits such as apples which have a preference in the British market. I have before me an article which appeared in the Financial Post on November 18 and the heading tells the story just about as clearly as the hon. member for Lincoln has told it. The article is headed:
Canadian canned fruits taken by British markets. Ocean steamship at St. Catharines takes entire cargo of pears and peaches canned by Canadian canners.
That is a very careful statement. The nouse will observe it does not say that the steamship takes an entire cargo of Canadian pears and peaches canned by Canadian canners. In the address which was made and to which this article was referring, the same being made by one of the officers of Canadian Canners, I note the speaker has been careful to make himself clear that the fruit was canned in Canada and not that it was of Canadian origin. I wish to make only one observation and it is this, that so far as the agreements are concerned, the statement of the hon. member for Lincoln clears up the point abundantly. The agreements do not give to Canadian producers of fruit for canning purposes any preference whatever in the British market. My hon. friend has made that quite clear. Certainly the agreement gives us a preference in the British market for fruit canned in Canada.
]Mr. Malcolm.]

I think my right hon.
friend will let me proceed when I am agreeing with the hon. member for Lincoln.

I rise to a point of order.

In deference to the

I was only answering

The speech of the hon. member for Lincoln is quite in accord with the facts in this instance, and it clears up any doubt in the mind of the house and should clear up any doubt in the minds of the people that any preference we are receiving in the British market for canned fruits and vegetables will be of benefit to Canadian labour and Canadian canners but will be of no direct benefit to Canadian fruit growers.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I rule that the discussion which has taken place is out of order.

Unemployment-Mr. Euler

In the hope that the fruit industry will survive the little storm which has raged so violently in the house for a short time, I desire to discuss in a more quiet atmosphere a question which is of great importance to the country, namely, that of unemployment.
I do so now with some embarrassment because I hesitate to prolong the proceedings and delay hon. members in returning to their homes.
In a consideration of the question of unemployment there are two factors which are outstanding in the minds of all members of the house: first, the duty of parliament and of the people of Canada to care for those hundreds of thousands of people who are not any longer able to care for themselves; and second, and this is infinitely more difficult, the necessity of finding the causes and devising a remedy for the position in which we find ourselves.
The Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) a few days ago gave to the house the information that there are now dependents on the bounty of the people of Canada no fewer than 850.000 people. That in itself constitutes to my mind a tragedy. Although I was aware, like other hon. members of the house, that there was a great deal of distress in the country, I was shocked at the magnitude of those figures. In view of the fact that in Canada there is plenty and the means of producing a great deal more, and that the same condition obtains in almost every civilized country of the world, it is a reflection not only upon civilization but upon Christianity, if you will, that such a condition should have arisen and should have continued to this day, with no real relief in prospect.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) some days ago said that we were moving toward a new economic order of things. I wish I knew exactly what was in his mind when he used those words. I believe he is right, but I wonder if he could explain to the house just what the nature of that movement is, and whether it is controlled, whether it is controllable, or whether we are merely drifting in a direction the end of which we do not know and cannot foresee.	_
The question of unemployment may fairly be divided into two main phases: First, the question of relief itself, which has nothing to do with the cure of unemployment; and secondly, the cure of the condition in which we now find ourselves.
So far as relief is concerned, every member of the house will join with the Minister of 53719-102
Labour when he says that there shall not be any man, woman or child in this country who will not be supplied with food, clothing and shelter. That may necessitate the taking from those who have and giving to those who have not. So far the debate on unemployment has confined itself mainly to methods of giving relief, which has nothing whatever to do with the cure of unemployment itself. Last year and the year before the method that was adopted by the government, in accordance with the policy of the Prime Minister that he was not going to hand out doles but proposed to give work to all who needed it, was this: Federally, to proceed with the construction of public works; provincially, helping some of the provinces, for example, in connection with the construction of a national highway, which project I imagine was not entirely as successful as it might have been; and municipally, through assistance received from the province and from the dominion a great deal of work was anticipated, that is, construction which might have been postponed for some years but was proceeded with then in order to provide employment. The difficulty was that the municipalities were called upon to spend such large sums of money that they have now arrived at a position where they can no longer pursue that course, and so, according to the Prime Minister, we have a request from the municipalities through the provinces, and from the provinces themselves that this year the relief shall take the form of direct assistance. I have no great fault to find with that, although of course I might say to the Prime Minister that he has been obliged to change his course. I might say to the Prime Minister in that regard, and to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) in connection with the debate that we had, that it is never safe for any man, least of all a public man, to make statements or promises that extend too far into the future, because conditions may arise necessitating a change of course of action.
We have now entered upon a new policy, a policy which I believe is hardly justified, and that is the policy, and I say it with some hesitancy, of making cash loans and cash advances to private corporations. My hon. friends will all understand to what I allude. I have no objection to means being provided so that men may be given employment, but I would draw to the attention of the government the fact that they are establishing a rather dangerous precedent. Generally I am not much given to considering precedents, even though my lawyer friends may be; but I think the government is placing itself in

Unemployment-Mr. Elder

rather an unenviable position when it advances help to one private corporation, which after all is conducted for profit, and which precedent will undoubtedly subject the government to demands, perhaps just as fair, from many hundreds of other sources which the government, I imagine, cannot concede.
I shall not say very much on the question of direct relief because it is largely a matter of efficient administration, to be handled on a non-partisan basis, with common sense and humanitarianism, and at that I am willing to leave it. But the question of direct relief has nothing whatever to do with curing the causes of unemployment. I propose to deal with the question, if I might say so, in the larger sense.
There are those who now say-we on this side have always said it-that unemployment and the condition in which we now find ourselves is largely attributable to world causes and that it obtains throughout the civilized world. That is true. But it does not follow that as a nation we cannot take certain steps which will at least alleviate or ameliorate the present condition. This I think we may as well lay down as a basic requirement before the world can return to prosperity: it must escape from the tremendous debt resulting from the war and in which perhaps our friends in the United States constitute the chief and deciding factor. These debts must be reduced or cancelled, and more than thait the world must get away from the spirit of war, that spirit which today, despite the League of Nations which was organized for the prevention of war, in Europe alone prompts the spending in preparation for another war of no less than about $5,000,000,000.
There is another condition of which we must rid ourselves. I refer to that feeling of patriotism, or that false doctrine-yes, I will call it a false doctrine-which leads nations to surround themselves with unscalable tariff walls. That is done in many instances with the idea of patriotism, which expresses itself in that way. Not only that, but in many countries patriotism seems to imply not only a love of one's own country but a hatred of or antagonism towards another. I said a minute ago that these are world conditions which must be dealt with. When one looks upon Europe today, considers the temper of European countries and of countries in South America which are on the verge of war, one is at once aware of the difficulties with which the world has to cope before improved conditions may be brought about.

I had intended to touch upon the problem from a Canadian standpoint, and what can be done by Canada itself to relieve ourselves from the excessive condition of unemployment around us. To my hon. friends in the corner of the house may I say that for about three years, since the beginning of the depression, I have listened to them and learned to regard them with a good deal of admiration. Sometimes I have envied them their attitude of certainty. Lately, when I have listened as they have given to the house the benefit of their advice as to what could be done to relieve us from the conditions under which we are suffering-and I am not saying this in any critical sense-I have regarded them with a feeling of inferiority, for I did not feel so sure as they do as to the remedy. However, when I learned two or three weeks ago thait a greater man, perhaps, than most of us, Sir Montagu Norman, Governor of the Bank of England, had, figuratively speaking, thrown up his hands and admitted that he did not know what to do, I felt that my self respect had been more or less restored. That does not mean after all that we should do likewise, but it does mean that he confessed his ignorance and humility just as I am doing now, by inference.
I feel, after all, that we might discuss in a more or less hopeful vein some of the things we could do. There is one matter which has been mentioned frequently by hon. members in the corner of the house and in connection with which I must again admit a lack of knowledge and, if you like, an ignorance-I am referring to the matter of currency reform. All I should like to say in that connection is that when we have a condition, under the system as it now obtains, whereby a man who three years ago created a certain debt now has to pay it three times over, having regard to the value he receives for his commodities, then certainly something must be wrong. What the remedy is I do not know. Our friends in the corner of the house recommend inflation. Sometimes I am not quite sure just what inflation means, and I imagine that many hon. members in the house, if they speak their minds, would admit a similar lack of knowledge.
Perhaps the Prime Minister has now come to the conclusion that a certain degree of inflation may be advisable. With the issue of $35,000,000 more of currency I believe inflation has been started at least in some degree. Further, the other day the Prime Minister admitted something I believe he had never admitted before, namely that we are no longer on the gold standard.

Unemployment-Mr. Eider

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh yes, he had.

If I may say so, my mind is quite open with regard to the matter and, if the Prime Minister and his government should see fit to enter upon a reasonably controlled degree of inflation, I am inclined to believe that I should support them.
Another matter which has been brought to the attention of the house by the labour members is that concerning shorter hours, a condition closely linked up with the introduction of labour saving machinery. Although we term such machinery "labour saving machinery," perhaps it should not be so called.
I may be wrong in that respect, but I fear that often such machines have not worked out entirely to the benefit of those operating them. Certainly in every constituency which is industrially organized, such as my own city of Kitchener, the introduction of labour saving machinery has literally replaced thousands of men. I am not opposed to the introduction or the development of machinery. I do not believe we should discontinue its use.
I do not believe it is good for a man to labour from early morning until late at night, ten hours, nine hours or even eight hours a day, if machinery can be made to do the work the man formerly did. I believe it would now be possible, if men were put to work with the machinery at our disposal, and through the medium of machines which will be invented in the future, to produce by four or five hours of labour each day sufficient to meet the requirements of all the people. Under those conditions it would be right for the working man to enjoy the leisure which undoubtedly would be his, a leisure which could be devoted to recreation or amusement, or for the benefit of body and soul, if you wish to put it that way. I believe in that. I have no doubt that one of the remedies and one of the results which must come from the introduction of machinery will be shorter hours of labour. I realize that the introduction of machinery and shorter hours presents many problems, some perhaps international, but at this time I shall not dwell upon them.
Then, there is another remedy which the present government has tried with, I suggest, no satisfactory results; I refer to extremely high tariffs. With that point I shall not detain the house long. My position in relation to tariffs is well known. I am not in favour of extremely high tariffs, and I believe even now members of the government will admit that as a factor in the cure of unemployment the introduction of extremely high tariffs has not 53719-102J
been a success. It has not been successful in creating greater purchasing power within the country. Further, since higher tariffs have been in force our foreign trade has declined from a position of fifth in world trade to that of seventh.
Would the hon. member be satisfied if the farmers of Canada worked, only four or five hours a day?

I should be very happy if they could operate their farms in that way. Perhaps it can be worked out. I should not attempt to do so, however, because I am not an expert. On the other hand, if they were able to do that I should be pleased, because I do not play favourites.
I was going to suggest that it might be possible to do something by way of controlling production. By that I do not imply that there is overproduction. I believe there will never be overproduction so long as the wants of every individual are not satisfied. I was directing my attention to another phase of the matter, and thinking particularly of the organization of industries for which there is^ no necessity. I refer particularly to overexpansion of industry. The example which: occurs to my mind is that of the manufacture of paper. For many years there was sufficient equipment in Canada for all the business in: this commodity we could get, and yet there-were people, men who were not "paper people," but promoters, who went into the field, organized new companies and built new mills which since have gone into the hands of the receivers, and the investors' money has been lost. The suggestion I was going to make to my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and it is more or less casual, is whether it would not be in the interests of the Canadian people that the Department of Trade and Commerce should have a branch which would devote itself to the acquisition of knowledge and information with regard to all lines of business, and particularly manufacture, in Canada; so that the investing public might have some means of ascertaining whether the business in which they are asked to invest their money has any chance for success. It might be possible to go even further, to work out a scheme with the provinces whereby if upon investigation it were shown that there really is not room for the investment of further capital in any particular line of business, a charter could be refused.
Then we have the remedy-or rather not a cure but a palliative-of unemployment

Unemployment-Mr. Euler
insurance. I favour unemployment insurance, as I think does every member. The Prime Minister has declared himself in favour of such a measure. He stated that it was delayed last year until compilation oould be made from the census reports. I think that time has now arrived, and I suggest to him that the government concern itself with the working out of an adequate system of unemployment insurance.
I wish to make another suggestion, which is not original, but of which I read a few days ago in the Saturday Evening Post. It might be called the rationing of work; to ration work just as food and fuel were rationed during the war. I will read a short extract and leave it as a suggestion to the government for inquiry.- The article is headed:
Job Spreading by Job Sharing
It goes on to say;
Now that the share-the-work movement is in operation from coast to coast and, has set up a regional organization in each federal reserve district, it cannot be premature to direct attention to the accomplishment it already has to its credit and to point out its possibilities as an engine for preventing the further spread of unemployment.
The basic idea of tiding the unemployed over present hardships by employing more hands for fewer hours a day or fewer days a week is simplicity itself; but its application to scores of differing trades and industries, each of which has requirements inseparable from its nature, is anything but simple.
The specifications for any sound plan for hastening business recovery demand that it be to the common advantage of three overlapping but still different groups,-the employers, the employed, and the general public. The share-the-work movement appears to meet this threefold requirement, and its sponsors seem fully warranted in declaring that it helps the employer because work spreading hastens business recovery; that it is to the advantage of the worker because job sharing makes for job security; that the public benefits because spreading employment means spreading spending power and the feeling of confidence and security that follow in their train.
I appreciate that that is not a cure, but it might be of some assistance.
Now I am going to venture for a moment upon a subject my attitude concerning which may be misinterpreted. If so, so much the worse for me. It rests upon what has become more or less a platitude, that while the world has solved the problem of production, and can produce sufficient for every man, woman and child, especially in Canada, it has not solved the problem of distribution; in other words, that which is produced is concentrated more or less in a few hands. I discussed this question a few days ago with one of my friends, and when I stated my thought with

regard to it he said: "That is the Karl Marx doctrine." Well, I must admit, perhaps to my discredit, that I have never read the works of Karl Marx. But this theorem or principle does appeal to me; that wealth, generally speaking, is produced almost entirely by the application of labour to natural resources, whether it be on the farm, in the factory, the mine, the stream or the forest. I make due allowance for management, transportation and so on-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And capital.

Yes, I will include capital in a reasonable way. If then it is found that there are great accumulations of wealth in a few hands, and poverty and distress obtain among the workers who have produced it, surely it is fair to assume that the spread between the man who has and the man who has produced is greater than it should be; in other words that capital is receiving too large a share of that which is produced.

Take care of the iron
heel!

We are faced with the problem of better distribution. I am inclined to think that hardly a member in this house does not believe in the accuracy and fairness of what I have said. But how are we to obtain better distribution? That of course is a difficult question. There are those who say- I think we have some in the corner-that we ought to scrap the present capitalistic system. I am not here to advocate that. Others say we should modify the system we now have, and I believe that at least for the present we ought to try that out. That we must do something I am convinced. Whether it shall take the form of taxation of profits, of profit sharing in industry, which already obtains in some industries managed by far-seeing and humanitarian leaders, I do not know. I read some time ago-perhaps my hon. friends in the corner will be interested in this from the Labour press, although they probably read it long before I did-an editorial in a Labour magazine. It said that the working people were already convinced that socialism is coming, in fact were so fully convinced of it that they were sitting more or less with folded hands waiting for it to come. The article went on to say that the editor himself was not in favour of the application of socialism now, because people were not ready for it. He hoped that the capitalistic system, which he seemed to think was more or less staggering. ought to be restored for the time being, and in the interval between the present and

Unemployment-Mr. Euler
the coming of socialism the Labour people and the public generally should prepare themselves for the duty of making the system operative when the proper time arrived. Now,
I am not a socialist, but the mere fact that a man believes in certain principles in which socialists also believe does not necessarily make him a socialist. Here again my selfrespect is restored when I hear men like Sir Josiah Stamp state in a speech which he made in the parliamentary restaurant that perhaps the remedy for the ills from which we were suffering lies somewhere between our present system and that which they have today in Russia. I should hardly have dared to go as far as that, but if I did I would be in pretty good company; I could cite other prominent economists also. The word "socialism" has no particular terrors for me, although, as I say, one's attitude is apt to be misinterpreted. I read the other day, or someone was telling me, about a book which in the time of the Czar someone attempted to introduce into Russia. The title of the book, I think, was The Dynamics of Sociology, and the officers at the border refused to let the book enter because they thought the word "dynamics" indicated that it had something to do with dynamite and the blowing up of the present system, and "sociology" indicated that it was to teach socialism. I cite that as showing that we have a fear of something just because of its name when as a matter of fact we have the thing already.
A fear of words.

We allow ourselves to be
handicapped by the fear of words. We have in Canada a system that is socialistic in a certain sense. The municipality from which I come owns the waterworks, the electric light plant, the gas plant, the street railway-
And liquor?

No, not in the municipality I come from. I can see the direction in which my hon. friend's mind is running. But we have all these things, and I will say to my hon. friends in this house in whose localities the principle of public ownership has not made the same progress as it has in mine, which is of course, the most progressive community in Canada, that it has been extremely successful. These services have been given the people of that community at a low cost and in just as efficient a manner as they could have been given by any private business. Provincially we have the great hydro system which in the past has been a great boon to the people of Ontario, and which I hope will carry on in the same way
in future. We also own a railway running from the city of Toronto to James bay. Let me say this also, though I am afraid it will not meet with the approval of some hon. members of this house:	The success of the
hydro in Ontario would not have been possible but for the fact that it is a monopoly.
I have no patience with those newspapers and individuals who constantly say that we want no monopoly, either public or private; that all monopolies are bad. I have said before in this chamber that a public monopoly loses the sinister features of a private monopoly, because it is conducted on an entirely different basis and for an entirely different purpose. The purpose of private ownership, of course, is profit, while the purpose of public ownership is service at as low a cost as possible. The inducement for the abuse of privileges in a public monopoly is not present as it is in a private monopoly. We also have in Ontario, as well as in every other province in the dominion, the public control of the traffic in liquor, and I am inclined to believe that this works a great deal better than was the case when it was in private hands. In the dominion we have had the post office for many years; that is a socialistic activity, if you like to call it that, and we have the Canadian National Railways.	.

That is a
tough one.

I suppose hon. gentlemen
will say, as my colleague from South Waterloo (Mr. Edwards) says, that this is a tough one. I do not intend to say much about the Canadian National Railways, though I am very much interested in them. If the national railways are in difficulties they are in just about the same condition as their great private competitor, and I think those difficulties are largely the result of the failure of private ownership. In my opinion-and here I know I am treading dangerous ground-if the national railways had the same monopoly of the railway business that the hydro has in that business in Ontario, we would have a successful system today.

Under the
same kind of management, perhaps.

Under a good government
it would have that management. Some eight years ago, Mr. Speaker, I had the temerity to make the suggestion in this house that it would be worth while for the government of Canada-and it was a Liberal government at that time-to make a canvass of the whole railway situation, with a possible view of the
Unemployment-Mr. Euler

amalgamation of the two great roads. I made the statement then, and I had it on very good authority, that we could save at least $75,000,000 yearly by the cutting out of wasteful competition. Not long ago, before the Royal Commisison on Railways and Transportation, Mr. Beatty, president of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, stated that a saving of $65,000,000 a year could be effected by the amalgamation of the two roads, and if that had been done at that time, in the ten years that have elapsed we -could have saved possibly three-quarters of a billion dollars, or about one-third of the *national debt.
I had not intended to go into this matter very deeply, Mr. Speaker, but as I said at the outset of my remarks, it is never very safe to make too definite statements, especially if you are in public life, or too definite promises as to what you may do in the future, and when I say that I am not referring to the promises made by the Prime Minister in regard to unemployment. I am referring to the slogan, if you like to call it that, which the Prime Minister nailed to the mast during his campaign. In connection with the railways he said, "Amalgamation never; competition ever." I believe that before very long the Prime Minister will have to reverse that slogan, because if we continue as we are going at present in connection with the two railways, with the consequent waste, this country will not be able to bear the burden.
I am out of order, perhaps, but I should like to make just a reference to the recommendations made by the royal commission. They advocate compulsory cooperation. This may be the only thing that can be done, but I will say that I have no great faith in compulsory cooperation; the two things just do not go together. I say further that in the future we will find the old slogan "competition is the life of trade" out of date; in certain respects at least competition is the death of trade and of prosperity. I hope that in future the slogan of Canadians and of the world will be cooperation rather than competition.
The question now is how far we can go in the direction of these socialistic tendencies, if you like to so call them. I am not prepared to say. It has been suggested that we should have a national bank, and that may be a good suggestion. It has been suggested also, and I am rather inclined to favour the suggestion, that we should at least mutualize our life insurance companies, and there may be many other directions in which we might proceed. The point I want to make, however, is that fMr. Euler.]
I believe some modification of our present system is necessary. We may survive the present difficulties; after a while we may turn that mythical corner of which we have heard so much, around which we will find prosperity. I do not desire to be pessimistic, but I am a little afraid it may be some time before we turn that corner. Whether or not that is so, however, some time later we will have another period of depression, and that will happen again and again unless we modify our system.
Some people think depressions are absolutely necessary under our capitalistic system. I do not believe that, but if it be so, then so much the worse for our system. In the olden days people believed that epidemics of smallpox, yellow fever and other diseases were dispensations of Providence, but science has overcome those epidemics. It does seem to me that it should not be regarded as inevitable that these alternate periods of depression and prosperity should exist in a country such as Canada. I feel that whether or not we see the way clear, at least we should make some effort to find a remedy. If there is one thing in the public mind at this time-and this applies not only to the people who have not very much by way of money or possessions but also to every member of this house, as it applies to myself- it is the constant fear of the future. We do not know what the future will bring, yet we are living in a country and in a world that can and should produce enough for everyone if that production is properly distributed. Surely there must be men of ability in this country, men of good will if you like, men like those who accomplished wonders during the development of the world's civilization, who can find a remedy, so that we should not regard ourselves as impotent to make further advances in the direction we desire to go.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, although I have made one or two tentative suggestions which possibly may be quite valueless, I admit, that I do not know the exact course of procedure which will bring about that which we all desire. During last session the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) proposed a resolution providing for the appointment of a committee or commission which would look into questions of this kind and present its findings and advice to the government. As I recall it, that resolution was passed by the house and accepted1 by the government, and I would suggest that action be taken along the lines suggested. Hon. members opposite, including the Prime Minister, have asked for

C.N.R.-Snow Removal from Gaspe
tbe cooperation of members of parliament in the difficulties through which we are passing. The Prime Minister has a right to make that request; I think it is our duty to extend that cooperation just so far as may be possible, and I was going to make this suggestion entirely on my own responsibility, unless the Prime Minister accepts the one I made with regard to the resolution adopted last year: the Prime Minister might very well consult with the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the leaders of the parties to my left in connection with the appointing of a committee. This committee could consist of certain hon. members of this house, augmented and supplemented1 by men in the country from whom we could obtain information or inspiration and advice. This committee would have the power of investigation and of forming settled opinions so that some sort of program might be drafted which would tnable us to proceed in the promotion of that condition to which we would like to return or which we would like to reestablish. It might be found that such a committee would prove to be of real assistance to the Prime Minister when he goes to the next world conference or succeeding world conference upon the deliberations and recommendations of which may depend the prosperity of the world in general and Canada in particular.

Mr. Speaker, under the privilege which we have under this motion to go into supply, I wish for a moment to comment upon the publicity given to the evidence of Mr. Appleton, head of the Atlantic region of the Canadian National Railways, before the Duff commission. The summary of this evidence appears in the Montreal Gazette. In dealing with the various branch lines throughout the maritime provinces, Mr. Appleton made the statement that one year it cost a million dollars to remove the snow from the Gaspe line. This statement is so preposterous that I cannot believe it was made by Mr. Appleton. I have been requested by the people in my district to correct any impression which may have been created in respect to this particular line. Snow removal upon this line costs no more than it does on other lines. Some winters we have very little snow, at times the first snow not coming until the middle of January. I think it is only fair to the people in this district to correct any impression which may have gone abroad that this particular branch line of the Canadian National Railways is being maintained at such a tremendous cost.

Mr. Speaker, for two or three days we have been discussing the questions of unemployment and farm relief. These two questions are somewhat related and until we can bring about a reasonable return to the farmers for the expenditure and cost of production, we will have an unemployment problem upon our hands. In anything I say this afternoon I do not wish to be understood as condemning any policy because it has not brought about one hundred per cent results nor in advocating anything as a cure-all for our ills. It has been said again and again that the farmers are chronic kickers. There are always some people who are failures and who will complain even in the best of times, there are others who can make a success in the hardest of times and living under the worst of conditions.
The question of the return which the farmer receives for the produce he places upon the markets of this country or of the world has been studied scientifically and thoroughly by the Department of Agriculture. I should like to refer to certain figures which appear in bulletin number 159 issued by this department in 1932, and dealing with the cost of producing farm crops in the prairie provinces. This study of the costs of production was made with the idea of ascertaining just where the farmers could reduce their costs. The farmer must market his products in competition with the world, and even though he sells on the home market, it is necessary that costs of production should be reduced if at all possible. I intend to refer to the cost of producing wheat given in this bulletin, and then set over against those costs the prices received by the farmer. This study has been very thorough and I do not think anything like it has ever been attempted before, at least I have not come across anything as thorough. The study was made in cooperation with eight experimental farms, by thirty-one dominion illustration stations in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta and in addition a survey was made by private individuals in cooperation with the officials of the department. The cost of producing wheat for the period 1923 to 1930 is given as 64 cents per bushel for wheat after fallow. In the second year after wheat, the cost is given as 75 cents per bushel. These figures were obtained from the dominion experimental farms. In the case of the illustration stations in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, where there was a check of thirty-one stations, the cost of producing wheat after summer-fallow was 63 cents per bushel, and the cost for the second year after fallow, 76

I find thait the average return to the farmer in the three prairie provinces for the year 1930 was 44 cents per bushel. In other w'ords, they lost that year about two cents a bushel, but they got the bonus. In 1931 they got thirty-eight cents and the loss in that year was about eight or nine cents a bushel. This year, without any reduction in cost below the 1930 figure, we have an estimate of what is actually reaching the farmers on the average grain on their farms, of twenty-five to twenty-nine cents a bushel. In other words, the farmers have been losing from eight to twenty cents during the last two years. If we take the figures from 1923 to 1929, we find that the farmers were making a profit of about fourteen or fifteen cents a bushel and things were going fairly well in Canada at that time. But that was not an exorbitant profit; it was a reasonable profit.
The question may be asked, and asked quite fairly, whether, because of the prosperous conditions we enjoyed from 1923 to 1930, the farmers should not have been able to stand the gaff, as some people say, in the last two years. Even the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) has raised the question why the farmers were in difficulties during 1930 considering the total value of their production in the preceding few years. There was issued by the Imperial, economic committee, volume

twenty, on the wheat situation, 1931, and at page 111 there is a statement taken, I believe, from tables prepared by the statisticians in Great Britain showing the relative value of wheat as compared with other commodities in Great Britain. The figures may not apply strictly to Canada, but I do not think that we have any figures worked out on this basis in this country. These figures are given over the period from 1846 to 1930. In 1846 we start off with 100, and if you follow the course of the value of all commodities in Great Britain, excluding wheat and flour, and the value of wheat in terms of other commodities, you will find that the value of wheat has been sliding down steadily ever since 1846. I think it is fair to say that it costs a little more to produce cattle under farm than under range conditions. Further, we ought to call attention to the fact that these are prices on the range, not on the market. It would cost probably SI per 100 pounds to get a lot of that stuff on to the market. So, while there has been a drop of possibly 30 per cent in the price of feed grains, it would still be necessary, in order to pay the cost of producing these animals, the cost of getting them to the market and the feed, to get about five cents a pound. I have under my hand a statement in the monthly bulletin of agricultural statistics for September, 1932. I am taking the quotations at Calgary and Edmonton of steers up to 1.050 pounds common. In Calgary they were selling from $3.50 per 100 pounds in May to $2 in August. That is the lowest figure given. That is the problem. They are returning about 40, 50 or 60 per cent of the cost of production. You lose on the production of wheat; you lose on the production of cattle if you feed the wheat to cattle. That is the story.
What about hogs? I do not want to take time or to weary the house, but I should like to give just a few figures taken from the report of the superintendent at the experimental station at Lacombe, Alberta, and I have checked them against figures of Ontario and further east in Canada. The cost of producing hogs in 1930 at Lacombe was $6.50 per 100 pounds for feed alone, nothing for labour, nothing for depreciation of buildings, nothing for the cost of carrying on the parent stock. That is given at page 36 of the report of the superintendent for 1930. Let us take bacon hogs. The price of hogs at Calgary was $3.37 in May and $4.08 in August. That might bring back the feed cost of production
if we allow for the fact that feed has dropped in price a little from 1930. At Edmonton the price of bacon hogs was $3.25 in May and $3.92 in August. It is the same story there.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the agricultural problem. What are we going to do about it? Prices have not gone up to any very great extent since August of this year. In fact, some have come down. Wheat has come down, and there does not seem to be any bottom to the wheat market. I have here a statement prepared by the Imperial Economic Committee. In its twentieth report on The Wheat Situation, at page 105, it shows the approximate wheat stocks in important areas from August 1, 1921 to August 1, 1932 as follows:

There was a little drop down in wheat stocks during the year 1931, but while I do not want to take time to quote the figures I may say that that was more than made up this year. We have wheat stocks in the world to-day of approximately 1,000,000,000 bushels, and available for export possibly 700,000,000 bushels. So I submit that whatever the government may do-I think the government was wise in the steps it took to support the wheat pool in marketing our western wheat, and I want to give the government credit for that-in face of the vast oversupply of wheat that we have in the world today there is no possibility of raising the price, and we might as well face that fact. It is no use handing out statements to the press that we have marketed a few more million bushels of wheat over a certain period than we did over a similar period in a former year and so on, so long as we have a huge surplus hanging over the world that we cannot gel rid of. Nor can you raise prices of cattle or hogs so long as you have a huge surplus hanging over the market. 'When we were discussing the trade treaties I said then that you cannot raise prices while you have huge surpluses pressing on the buying market all the
