Farm Relief-Mr. Kennedy (Peace River)
time. You cannot do it. If we are to save our present social system or save it long enough till we can change it for something better there must be a reasonable increase in prices, and the question of raising prices is not altogether a question of raising the value. Prices is a purely relative term. If we cannot raise prices in the world's markets we can decrease the cost of production, and decrease the value of money in relation to the price of wheat, thereby making our produce worth more in relation to money. That is the only thing we can do.
It has been argued that the value of gold is always the same. Yes, it is, in relation to gold, but not in relation to anything else. Just as motion is a purely relative thing, so is value, and the only thing I can see to do in this regard without advocating inflation and increasing the volume of credit or money, or whatever you like to call it, is to lower the value of money in relation to our commodities. It is the flow of money or credit or whatever you like to call it in accordance with the law of supply and demand that determines the value of money in relation to all your commodities. That same law applies to money just the same as it does to wheat or anything else. But the world has been restricting credit in spite of the gold basis. Take what has happened in the United States, which country we have been trying to follow to some extent here in Canada. I have a report of an address here which was made by Donald M. Marvin, Ph.D., economist of the Royal Bank of Canada, in which he sets forth what happened in the United States about 1929. He says:
In the months which followed the clash in security prices the volume of world trade declined steadily, and prices fell. As gold accumulated in the creditor countries, France and the United States, these countries did not increase their volume of outstanding credit; they permitted it to continue to contract. Even in recent months the weekly returns of the member banks in the United States show a decline in loans and investments of $1,000,000,000 since the first of November; $2,000,000,000 since the last of September, and $3,000,000,000 since April, 1931. The decline in the first four months from October has been at the rate of $6,000,000,000 per year, or more than 25 per cent per annum. No nation can stand such a contraction of credit.
While there may have been contraction or a drop in prices due to the fact that other countries were doing similar things, the contraction in Canada and the United States was also a factor, and a big factor, in the crash of commodity prices.
One reason why we want to see the dollar go down to the level of the pound is that

it will mean that our commodities that we must sell on the basis of world prices will be worth more in relation to debts and in relation to the cost of production. We do not advance that as a cure-all. If we did we might well be laughed at. There will still be a lot of problems to be solved even after that is done. I do not think the government is taking the wise course in relation to the primary producers of this country in trying to keep the dollar up as high as possible. Somebody has to sacrifice, and I think the farmer has sacrificed in the last few years. I have advised the farmers throughout my constituency, notwithstanding the fact that I could not see any prospect in the near future of an improvement in conditions to any great extent, at least until this money question was tackled, in spite of the fact that the treaties are of some value and will do some real good, to continue on as carefully as possible because it is their duty to Canada to carry on. If the primary producers of this country were to throw up their hands, the bonds of the country and the savings of the people would not amount to much.
Some people take another position. The Prime Minister has taken it on one or two occasions, if I understood the reports of his speeches, namely, that because we ask for some inflation we are asking the government to do what they did in Germany and Russia during and after the war. Now if praying for rain means that you are praying for a flood, that would be all right; but it is not so. Our whole life is an attempt to regulate our conduct on the principle of moderation, a choice between two extremes. If it is right to argue that every man who takes a drink is a drunkard, it would be all right to argue that deflating the dollar to the level of the British pound would be asking the country to do what happened in Germany during the war. What happened in Germany? In December, 1920, they had 81 millard paper marks issued, and at that time 17 paper marks were worth one gold mark. In August, 1923, there were 116,000 millard paper marks issued, and it took 1,000,000 of them to equal one gold mark. That, Mr. Speaker, is inflation with a vengeance.
Then, turning to Austria we find that in June, 1920, there were 17 millard paper krone in circulation; at that time 27 paper krone were worth one gold krone. On August, 1923 there were 5,557 millard paper krone in emulation, and 14,369 were required to equal one gold krone.
Then follow the currency conditions in Russia. We find in January, 1919 there were

Farm Relief-Mr. Pouliot
61 millard paper roubles in circulation, and at that time 103 paper roubles equalled one gold rouble. In June, 1923 there were 8,050,000 millard paper roubles in circulation, and at that time 97.690,000 paper roubles equalled one gold rouble. These figures show the extent of inflation which obtained in Germany, Austria and Russia. What happened in those countries was that the savings of people holding wealth in titles to money were wiped out. Germany practically wiped out her internal debt. The same happened in Russia.
We do not want that to happen in Canada. The sensible basis upon which to regulate the volume of money-and it cannot be done without a central bank charged with responsibility-is in relation to price levels. Thereby one can issue a fair volume of money to the people who have saved up wealth, and a reasonably fair issue to the producers of commodities. That is the point at which we must aim. At present we are sacrificing the people who produce manufactured goods, and we are also sacrificing the farmers for the sake of those people who have wealth and titles to money. We are not asking the government to go to the other extreme, but merely asking for reasonable parity or equilibrium. There are other places also where parity might be established.
So, Mr. Speaker, that is one step which in my view' may be taken. Some people ask: How can it be done? The Macmillan committee advanced various methods of doing it, but I believe it could be done very simply if the Prime Minister would announce tomorrow in this house that Canada, for the future, would try to stabilize her dollar on a level w'ith the British pound, in relation to the United States dollar. I believe that would do it. Further, I believe anything done along that line, while it may take away from people who have wealth and titles to money, will make for better conditions generally among the whole population of Canada.
The hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) who spoke immediately before me referred to the doubts entertained by Sir Montagu Norman and several other gentlemen. Certainly there is one thing about which there can be no doubt, namely that we cannot continue to go on as we are doing today. We must go somewhere. What have been the experiences in countries which have devalued their money? Has Great Britain lost? Undoubtedly some people in Britain had to lose, but Great Britain has been able to balance her budget. - Further, if the figures given to the house by the hon. member for
Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) can be relied upon, and I believe they can, Great Britain has been able to show an increase in employment. She is maintaining her export business on the markets of the world better than any country that has chosen to remain on the gold basis. The United States, and several other countries on the gold basis, are losing heavily. Australia is operating on a devaluated currency. An editorial taken from an Ottawa Journal of recent date is as follows:
A loan floated by the government of New South Wales in October, guaranteed by the Commonwealth government, was over subscribed within half an hour. The loan was for thirteen million pounds, to bear three and one-half per cent interest, and was issued at ninety-seven. . . .
Professor Copland. of the Melbourne university School of Commerce, who is one of the Australian government's expert advisers, says that Australia has been saved by a threefold policy:
1.	Depreciation of currency in terms of gold. The exchange rate is now 25 per cent off sterling and 60 per cent off gold.
2.	Expansion of credit.
3.	Cutting of costs.
We have tried some of these things in Canada but not depreciated currency and expanding credit. We have been contracting credit although, I believe there has been some slight expansion lately. It is because I believe that will help in the present situation that I am advocating it to the house. I want to give the government full credit for what it has done in the marketing of wheat, although I wish it had been able to continue the bonus, because the need is desperate. If however the government cannot see its way clear to do that I think it is only fair that, in view of the tremendously difficult circumstances under which the farmers of western Canada are operating and for that matter all farmers, there should be a devaluation of the dollar, and, for a time at least, a sacrifice on the part of those people who in the last few years have received wealth by an increase in the purchasing power of their money without effort on their part. I believe they should be asked to make a sacrifice in order that primary producers may be helped, by a relative lowering of costs of production and debts.

Mr. Speaker, I regret I cannot
understand the attitude of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy) who has spoken before me. It would seem that he is dissatisfied with the government, and for that reason I cannot understand why he has voted with them.

I regret very much the absence from the house of the Prime Minister at this time. The present discussion concerns the situation now obtaining in Canada and I believe the Prime Minister should be in his seat to hear the complaints from the different constituencies.
Where is the leader of the opposition?
The leader of the opposition is not in charge of the government.
I see.
I believe the Prime Minister should follow the good example of the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion) and should be in his seat at the moment.

No; in due course the
Prime Minister will name them. A few days ago my distinguished friend from Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Casgrain) brought a matter of great importance to the attention of the house. At that time he spoke concerning the guarantee given by the government to the wheat pool. In the course of his explanation the Prime Minister uttered the following words which appear at page 1094 of Hansard:
If I might say so, I do not think any good purpose would be served by going into the details of the operations which we have entrusted to the organizations I have mentioned under the management of Mr. McFarland.
At that time I took the opportunity to make a practical suggestion to the Prime Minister. It appears as follows at page 1096 of Hansard:
As the right hon. gentleman has said that it would serve no good purpose to give any more details about the situation and as the explanations that he has already given are most interesting, would he have any objection to having the galleries cleared in order that he may give full information to the house? I have asked the Prime Minister for an answer.

I asked for an answer because the Prime Minister made no reply to my suggestion. Then Your Honour said "No." I note however that there was no answer from the Prime Minister. My point of view was this: We are here to look after the business of the country. At times it may have been that the government was a few millions up. At the moment the Prime Minister made his statement however I learned from a reliable source that the government was down about $30,000,000 or $40,000,000. Whether or not my information was correct I cannot say, but I was very suspicious when the Prime Minister refused to tell the house what had really happened. If he could not give that information to the press, he could very easily have the galleries cleared and given full information to the house so that we might have known the deficit in connection with that particular operation.
He has done that for the west; what has he done for the east? In that connection I asked him another question; I like to see him in the house so that I may ask him questions. As it is a one-man government, of course I can ask questions of only that one man. The other day I asked the Solicitor General (Mr. Dupre) to convey a message to the Prime Minister. I had to convey my message through Hansard, because the Prime Minister was not in his seat.
Probably the Solicitor General could not see the Prime Minister.

Oh, I believe he could see him; I shall give him the benefit of the doubt. According to Hansard of November 15, page 1155, I spoke as follows:
Whether it is good, or whether it is bad I am not yet ready to express a view,-
I was speaking about the guarantee to the wheat pool.
-but may I ask the government seriously to consider if it is not advisable to give the same warranty to the farmers who raise hogs, to those engaged in the dairying industry, in potato-growing, to those who have greenhouses, to those-
Mr. Chairman said: Order, and I continued:
If the move that has been made by the government with regard to guaranteeing wheat is a good move, it is just as good for the hog industry. The other day the right hon. Prime Minister was in Toronto, and may I quote a very short extract from the Mail and Empire of November 17, 1932. It is entitled:
Hordes of Yelling Children Surround Premier at Fair, Forcing a Strategic Retreat

Only one premier, but-
That is the subtitle; isn't this delightful?

And it explains that if he made a fair speech in the evening-he was speaking at the fair, it was necessarily a fair speech, but some of the statements were painful. We see in large characters as a headline in the Mail and Empire of November 17, what declaration, what statement?
Home Market Ensured Farmers, Bennett Asserts

One boy is married and lives away from home, and is unable to give any assistance. Of the seven girls one is working in another city and two are employed as maids. There are many government employees receiving small salaries, who suffered a cut of 10 per cent and who are supporting their married children who are unable to get work. Mr. THOMAS F. DONNELLY (Willow Bunch):	Mr. Speaker, we are, I hope drawing near to the end of this portion of the session. Hon. members who come from industrial centres will be going back home to their constituencies and the first question the labourer will be asking them will be:	What
have you done for the unemployed? They will have to admit that during the present session nothing has been done which will in any way help the unemployed. Those of us who come from the agricultural centres also will be going back home, and the first question our farmers will be asking will be: What have you done for the relief of the distressed farmer? We shall be obliged to admit that nothing whatever has been done during the present session to relieve unemployment and our distressed farmers.
With a government that went into power promising to end unemployment, promising the farmers a high price for their wheat, a high price for their butter and high prices for all their other farm commodities, unemployment, farm relief and the administration of those two matters should surely be their first consideration. Whatever we may say or think, throughout the length and breadth of the country these two problems, the relief of farmers and the giving of work to the unemployed, are uppermost in the mind of almost every Canadian.
Some hon. members will say:	This unemployment and this distress on the farm are due to the world, depression. We admit that. It was true in 1929; it is true today. The depression which has spread over different parts of the world has caused in other countries conditions similar to those obtaining here, but we believe the policy of the present government has aggravated the situation in Canada. If we study this depression, we find that it has followed the course of many others. Depressions have existed in Canada and in the world before, and they have all gone in the same direction. We find that the first people to feel the effect of hard times are the primary producers: the farmers on the land, the fishermen, the lumbermen and the miners, especially of the coarser metals. These people begin to get a smaller price for their 
product. The result is that their buying power is lessened, they are able to buy very little from the retail merchant. The retatil merchant in turn is able to buy very little from the wholesaler, and as a consequence the wholesaler is able to buy very little from the manufacturer. In about six months or a year the manufacturer begins to feel the lack of buying power on the part of the primary producer, whether he be farmer, fisher, lumberman or miner. Conversely, when we begin to come out of the depression, the first people to feel the effect of good times are^ the primary producers. They begin to get higher prices for their goods. The farmer receives a better price for his produce; the fisherman also, the miner a better price for his coarser metals and the lumberman, whether in pulp-wood or ordinary lumber, begins to get a better price. These better prices enable them to buy more from the retail merchant. As a result the retail merchant buys more from the wholesaler, and the wholesaler more from the manufacturer. This has been the course of every depression through which the world has passed, and doubtless the present one will follow the same course.
We find, however, today that instead of times getting better, day by day and week by week prices are getting smaller and smaller to the primary producr. We are getting further and further, deeper and deeper into the present depression, and in fact it looks as though there were no daylight ahead. We have never yet got over a depression by starting at the top and working down, by the manufacturer or the financier or the stockbroker getting better prices for stocks or shares or bonds. The movement always starts with the primary producer and we find that he is getting into a worse position day by day and week by week.
What is the cause of the present unemployment and farm distress? All economists throughout the world say today that the main cause of unemployment and farm distress is tariffs; that greed on the part of an individual, of a corporation, of a country and, coupled with that, anything which produces or constitutes special privileges handed out to individuals are the causes of our present depression. We find today, for example, that in western Canada we have conditions where our farmers are unable to grow wheat because it is too cheap. With wheat at from twenty-five to thirty cents a bushel our farmers cannot grow it because it is too cheap. Yet in Germany we find that the farmers cannot eat white bread because it is too dear. On the other hand, we find that the farmers in

Farm Relief-Mr. Donnelly
western Canada cannot buy iron or steel for the repair of binders or mowers or rakes or whatever it may be, because those commodities are too dear, whereas Germany cannot produce iron and steel because they are too cheap. The German common people and the common people of the west are willing to exchange our wheat for their iron and steel, but they are prevented from doing so. By whom? By the big interests, by politicians and by the policies of the different governments in placing restrictions in the way of high tariffs on our wheat going into Germany and their iron and steel coming into Canada. The result is that we are starving for the need of iron and steel for our repairs and Germany is starving for the lack of wheat. These are well known facts. I might say the same thing with regard to France, Italy, and almost every other country in Europe. Almost everyone today, even some hon. gentlemen opposite- the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Sutherland) in South Huron, and the hon. member for North Huron (Mr. Spotton), said they would like to see tariffs done away with- realize the proper course to pursue is to do away with tariffs. We would like to do away with tariffs, but everyone is afraid to make a beginning. They say: We cannot do that because all the world has gone crazy and we must be crazy too. Someone must make a beginning in the direction of lowering tariffs. If we were to start doing so, then we would be able to deal with other countries and make conditions better for our own farmers and labourers.
We in Canada live under a system of what we call individualism or capitalism. This has grown out of the old Norman system when each individual was supposed to be paid according to his work. He could work as long and as hard as he liked and put as much mental ability into his employment as he wished, and he was rewarded according to his labour. The idea was that every man should have freedom of action. Developing out of that we have the system of Cobden, Bright and Gladstone of freedom of action by a country, where we should have freedom of trade between countries, just as individuals have freedom of action. That is the history of the past. But we find at the present time that restrictions have been placed upon freedom of trade among nations and we find also that under our system there has not been a just reward for labour, I do not care whether it be that of the mine or sea or farm or office. Capitalism has been receiving too much; the manufacturer has been getting too great a reward for his capital. Unless some-53719-103
thing is done to give a more equitable reward to labour, there is no doubt that this capitalistic system of ours will break. Then the only thing left for us is communism, and no one wants communism in this country. As a matter of fact, we have it already in a measure in Canada. We are under communism when the state tells us what we are to work at, to get a living, clothing and warm beds. If you go to gaol or the penitentiary the country will give you a meal and a warm bed, but no one wants that condition. Our present system must be reformed, and if it is not reformed then as sure as day follows night our system as we know it today is going to break. I repeat, that this system does not work out perfectly either for the individual or for the country. In other countries we have seen people carried away by greed and selfishness.
I have sympathy with the Prime Minister because I do not think the manufacturers used him fairly, and I say that without fear of contradiction. When he came into power he did away with the tariff advisory board, and then the manufacturers came to him and told him that they wanted so much tariff on their goods.
I believe they asked for more then they needed. I believe that firmly, but the Prime Minister took them at their word and gave them what they asked. He gave them too much. These manufacturers asked for too much and they got too much. It is only human nature to ask for a lot and expect less. That was the way with the manufacturers, except that they asked for a lot and got a lot. It was this spirit of greed operating again. They were carried away by this trait in our human nature. But I say, Mr. Speaker, that granting them such high protection has helped to make conditions worse than they otherwise would have been. Personally I do not think that any manufacturing concern in Canada or anywhere else should receive more than 15 or 20 per cent protection at the most. A certain amount of protection perhaps should be given to some manufacturers, but when a manufacturer asks for 90 or 100 per cent protection he should not be given it. It is out of reason altogether. Yet these manufacturers asked for it and got it. The result is what? It means that our farmers have lost their buying power; they cannot buy as much as they could before. It means that the ordinary labouring man is thrown out of employment, and little by little the effects spread and intensify the present depression.
What do we find in regard to unemployment? Last year I had occasion where I was situated to see many of these men who were

Farm Relief-Mr. Donnelly

out of work and wandering up and down the country. I must disagree with the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) when he says that these men are mostly foreigners. I am sorry to say that most of them are Canadian-born, young men mostly between the ages of 16 and 24, who have left the farm and gone out into the world to try to make a living, and now find themselves out of work. It was these young men, Canadian born, who were in the majority of those that I found travelling up and down on our trains. When they left home and started out in the world to make a living they wandered about for a year or two, and I am sorry to say that the majority of them go from bad to worse, so that after a time it is hard to get them back into industrial life. Those are the conditions as I saw them in western Canada, at all events.
The only policy that the Minister of Labour seems to have to oure this condition is to put these people back on the land. I want to say this with regard to the back to the land movement: I have been farmiiNg in western Canada for the last 24 or 25 years and you can take any farmer in western Canada today, and let him be ever so good a farmer, put him on the best land in western Canada, and give him his home and the farm equipment he needs, and I will guarantee that he cannot make a living and pay his taxes. W hen men who have been at farming all their life are not able to make a living on the best farms in western Oanada today, why send these people out of our cities back to the land ? The best farmer in western Canada today, if you give him his land and his home, his horses and equipment, is not able to make a living and pay taxes on the land at present prices of fann products. I am still farming in western Canada and know whereof I speak. And when I see papers like the Winnipeg Tribune writing article after article saying that all is well in the west and that we are on the road to prosperity, I say, Mr. Speaker, that it is a shame. They are just armchair farmers sitting around the fire, not out doing the actual work on the farm, getting up at four or five in the morning. If they had to do that, they would realize what they were up against and what reward they got for their labour. They would know that conditions are as I have stated. They simply do not know whereof they speak. I repeat, the farmer in western Canada today, I do not care where he is, is not able to make a living and pay his taxes under present conditions.
I hope that some good will come out of the provincial conference which the Prime Minister has called, and that something will

be done whereby work will be provided for some of our people. It is a step in the right direction, and I want to congratulate the government for having taken it. I trust that something will be evolved that will enable our unemployed to get work.
Just to give the house some idea of farming conditions in western Canada, last summer a man on one of my farms was going into town and he thought he would take in a beef hide to sell. He put the hide into the car and drove into town. He went up to the merchant and asked him: "How much will you give me for this?" The merchant replied, "It is of no value to us." "Will you give me two bits for it?" the man asked. "No," said the merchant, "it is of no value to us." "Well," said the man, "will you take it if I give you two bits?" "Well no," the merchant replied, "as far as that is concerned, if you want to get rid of it I will take it from you, but it is of no value." So the man gave him the hide for nothing, a hide from a 700 or 800 pound steer. Then the man turned round and went across the street to the hardware merchant's, and bought for SI .50 a pound of lace leather made out of the very same raw material that he had given away for nothing.
That statement is absolutely wrong and misleading to the farmers of western Canada. You cannot make lace leather out of that, kind of hide.

I want to tell the hon. member that I have seen lace leather made out of hides of that kind. If the hon. member is a tanner he may know. I am not a tanner, but I have seen lace leather made out of that kind of a hide.
(Assiniboia): So have I.

Yes. I am not speaking from hearsay. I know whereof I speak. He paid 81.50 for one pound of lace leather, and the hide he gave away for nothing. WThat is true of that hide is true of other things. Only the other day a carload of feeders was sent down from western Canada to Toronto and sold to the farmers on the farms in eastern Canada. It was laid down outside of Toronto for two cents a pound. How much will the farmer in western Canada get for those cattle? About half a cent a pound. He cannot get more. The freight all the way from western Canada to Toronto and then out to the farms will eat up the other cent and a half, leaving the farmer in western Canada only half a cent a pound. That will give the house some idea of the prices the farmer is getting for his products. Freight

Farm Relief-Mr. Donnelly
eats up most of his returns. Some baby beef was sent into Winnipeg, and was sold for two cents a pound. One cent a pound was paid for freight and commission, with the result that the farmer received only one cent per pound for his product. That was his net return. On top of that he had to pay fifteen cents exchange on the cheque. Hon. members will readily see that farmers are receiving ridiculously low prices for their products. The result is that today it is impossible for the farmers in western Canada to exist and to pay taxes on their lands. The condition I am describing is general throughout the western provinces. At this point however I should like to refer to conditions in my own district.
I come from a part of western Canada which has been so unfortunate as to have had no crop for the last four years. This year we are in the same position; we have no crop. Conditions may be described as terrible. I have heard of famines in India, China, and other parts of the world, but the condition existing in my district is as bad as any famine which ever took place. I have lived in and practised medicine in Canada for many years. I have always said that I never saw a hungry farmer in western Canada; I never saw want or poverty before. But I must admit that in the last two years I have seen more want, more poverty and more hardships than I have known to exist in the world before. These are the conditions in my section of the country.
What has the government done to relieve these settlers? Many charitable organizations have sent out relief in the form of clothes, groceries, and one thing and another. The farmers in the stricken areas are thankful for the relief they have received. Provincial legislatures also have handed out a certain amount of relief, and I want the house to understand we are thankful for the relief we are given. On the other hand, what are we actually getting by way of relief? How much do we receive? I have in my hand a letter from a clergyman in my district which sets out what the farmers in western Canada are receiving to help them in their distress. According to his information an adult is receiving $7 a month, a boy $5 a month, a girl $4 a month, and a child under seven years of age $2.50. With this amount of money they must buy their clothing and their groceries- $7 a month for an adult. Anyone who stops to think must know that a man cannot buy the necessities of life with this amount of money, and with that in mind hon. members realize the distress that exists.
We feel that the cost of distributing relief is altogether too high. In every municipality there is a relief officer. He runs up and down from one town to another; I do not know what he does, or why he travels from place to place. The fact is, however, that he runs backwards and forwards and receives good pay for it. There is a whole army in Regina, and I shah endeavour later to tell what they do. On the reverse side of the relief orders handed out there is an indication as to what a man may buy.-a certain quantity of beans, tea, coffee, sugar, or other necessities of life-and the prices he must pay are set opposite. I will guarantee that when those orders are presented to the merchants not one in half a dozen is made out according to the list on the back,-no, not one in a thousand. I will guarantee there is not a merchant in western Canada today who lives up to the regulations appearing on the back of those orders. He fills in the order just as he likes, indicating so man,v pounds of beans, so much tea, and so on. According to these receipts, carloads of beans have been sold. The merchant fills in the order, then turns around, _ asks the farmer what he wants and gives it to him. For example, tobacco is not included in the list and we all know that every farmer who smokes will get tobacco. The result is that the farmer gets his tobacco, although it may not appear on the order.
In Regina an army of two or three hundred is working in connection with relief measures. What is their work? Their work is to go over these lists and see that they are made out properly. They see that the calculations appearing on the orders are correct, and that the right amount of sugar or flour has been handed out. They are employed in that way, although we know as a matter of fact that many of the entries on the backs of the orders aTe fictitious. Yet we find them figuring at it, and that is the work for which we are paying them. In my view we would do much better to write out a cheque and send it to the farmer, telling him at the same time that he will receive no more until the first of the next month. Under the present circumstances a farmer may want to buy a postage stamp, and has to have money therefore. Under those circumstances he would go to a merchant, hand him his relief order and say, "I want a dollar with which to buy postage stamps," or "I want to go to the drug store to buy a bottle of castor oil." Invariably the merchant hands out the dollar and charges it up to so many beans. That is the way it is done, all
Farm Relief-Mr. Donnelly

the way through. Despite the inaccuracy of it all, we are paying all these relief officers and assistants. For what? For nothing, that is all.
In connection with this problem of relief I have only one more point to make. I have often wondered why a bachelor, we will say, out on a farm on the prairies, who wants a crust of bread, a cup of coffee or a pound of butter, must, before he receives any of them, sign a note saying that he will pay. We talk about relief, but we are not receiving relief in western Canada. We are only being financed. I wonder if the Prime Minister considered he was granting relief when he loaned money to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, or if he considered that he was merely financing. That is all he is doing with us; he is just financing us. For every dollar we receive in western Canada we have to sign on the dotted line, saying that we will pay. Why should we be treated differently from other parts of the country? What is the practice in the cities? When a man in the city of Ottawa states that he is hungry and wants a meal, do you make him sign a note before you send him to a soup kitchen? Why should you make the farmer in the west sign a note? I am not talking about seed grain;
I am not talking about relief handed out by way of feed for horses, or that sort of thing;
I am referring to ordinary grocery bills and the necessities of life. In order to get ordinary pork and beans with which to sustain life the western farmer has to sign a note, a promise to pay.
I do not know whether the same practice i3 followed in Ontario or in Manitoba, but I know it is done in Saskatchewan, and is being done to day. When I asked the Prime Minister why this practice was followed he said:	''II hy, I was flooded with telegrams
from people in western Canada begging that they be allowed to sign notes." But when I asked him for a copy of those telegrams I could not get them, and so far they have not been forthcoming. I have gone all through the west and questioned farmer after farmer, man after man, to find just who had sent those telegrams. I could not find any of them;
I do not know who sent them. I heard one farmer say if he ever caught hold of the man who admitted sending one of those telegrams it ovould be a sorry day for him, that he would make it most uncomfortable for him. They believe they are being descriminated against. They believe their hard times are being made worse.
Another thing we in the dried out areas had to contend with was the relief measures handed

out by this government by way of wheat bonus. That was one of those half-baked pieces of legislation put through last year by the government. At first it was going to be so much a bushel, five cents, on export wheat, but that was modified time after time until we got five cents per bushel of wheat sold by the farmer. What relief would that be to the farmers in a dried out district in which no crop was produced? We got none of it whatever. The only thing it did for us was to make us pay five cents a bushel more for our seed wheat. We had to pay more for our flour on that account. There were some seventy to one hundred municipalities in the same condition, which got no benefit whatever from this bonus. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) took great credit to himself last year in connection with this wheat bonus. He said he came down here and told the Prime Minister that this was to be a compensating adjustment for the tariff, and prevailed upon the Prime Minister to give him the bonus. This was to be compensation to the farmers for the increased prices they would have to pay on their purchases on account of the tariff. I want to know if the Minister of Agriculture is using his persuasive powers on the Prime Minister again to get a bonus. We dp not want a bonus on wheat. Of course I am glad to see these people get the higher price; we know that in the north the people had a production of forty and fifty bushels an acre and some of them received S2 or $2.50 an acre through the bonus. We do not begrudge them that, but we sajr that we in the south who had the same trouble putting in our crops and got nothing are also entitled to something. We believe this bonus should have been so much per acre seeded to wheat. It came just at the time when this could have been done without any trouble whatever. The census had just been taken; every fanner had stated the amount of land that he had in wheat; all the government had to do was to take the acreage and say: it is going to be fifty cents or $1 an acre. But instead, the principle was invoked: "he that hath, shall be given, and he that hath not, from him shall be taken even that which he hath." It is the same policy carried out by this government all the way through-the man who is rich gets more; the poor man is made poorer. Here is the man with a crop getting $1.50, $2, $2.50 an acre, and the man without a crop having to pay more for his seed.

What about the relief they got ?

Farm Relief-Mr. Campbell

I have just spoken about that, for every nickel of relief we had to sign on the dotted line saying we are going to pay it back. Did you sign cm the dotted line for the five cents a bushel bonus, and promise to pay it back? I did not get any of that relief because I did not have any crop, but I bad to pay five cents a bushel more for my seed this year.
All the money I have is invested in land in western Canada, and that land today is not worth anything. Our Prime Minister and the government have not the farmer's viewpoint, not one of them. The Prime Minister has the viewpoint of the industrialist and the capitalist. I am anxious that he should see something of the farmer's viewpoint. If he would do a little farming he would know something of the farmer's difficulties. I will make him an offer. I have four half sections of land, 320 acres each. Two of them are encumbered and two of them are clear. I want to give one of these half sections to the Prime Minister, provided he will farm it for the next five years. I do not say he has to go on the farm himself, but he can have it farmed for the next five years and show each year the return he gets. Farm land is not worth anything today; it is a liability rather than an asset, because you have to pay taxes on it. For the last three years I have not received one dollar by way of return from that $125,000 invested in farm land in western Canada. That is the condition that exists there now. I say to him that if he is going to take this land he should take one of the half sections that is encumbered, because then he will know what the average farmer has to contend with. The average farmer in western Canada has his land encumbered. Let him farm it; let him see what they have to put up with. He can farm it in one of three ways: with oxen, with horses, or with gasoline. I would advise him to go back to the oxen, because if he tries to use gasoline he will have to pay duty on it, and he will find it very expensive. This is just a digression, but I make the offer to the Prime Minister in good faith, and I am willing to turn the land over to him at any time he wants it.
Oh, oh.

Someone over there is
talking; I can give him a half section too. There are four of them, and he can have any one of them.
And make money!

Well, you are a better
man than I am. I have noticed that people
in eastern Canada know more about farming in western Canada than the man who is living there. But I notice, too, that the man who comes from eastern Canada has to spend two or three years in the west before he knows anything at all about farming. The farmers in the west are the most up-to-date in the world, bar none. We do not need anyone from the east to tell us how to farm. We are through with these armchair farmers who go through the country telling the western farmers from the back of an observation car how to farm. All we want is that they get off our backs and give us an even chance. We sell in the markets of the world, and we want to buy as freely as we sell. If they get off our backs and let us do that we will make good. That is the trouble today. Do you know that in western Canada we have been importing, from 1925 to 1930, about $200,000,000 worth of manufactured goods a year from eastern Canada? The duty we have had to pay on these goods is somewhere about 25 per cent. In short, we have been paying 25 per cent more on those goods than we should, and we have been paying that to eastern Canada, an average of $50,000,000 a year. What does that mean? It means that when I go out on the farm and thresh my wheat, I thresh three loads and sell it to the elevator, and it is mine, but the fourth load I have to give to the industrialists of eastern Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the various phases of farm relief have been so well and so ably covered by the speakers who have preceded me in this section of the house that I will confine my remarks entirely to one feature of what I consider farm relief.
In dealing with a change in the money system I do not for a moment suggest that this will be a cure for all our ills. As long as the world depression remains as it is, as long as world markets are demoralized, as long as Europe remains the armed camp that it is today, as long as the dark shadow of international debts overhangs the world, I know that there is very little that can be done by this parliament or this government to create better markets in Europe. But I do believe that there are some measures of relief that we can introduce here that will at least alleviate the situation to a great extent. I believe that certain changes in our monetary system will give a large measure of relief, particularly to the agricultural industry, and to a lesser de-
Farm Relief-Mr. Campbell

gree perhaps to all other lines of business. Twenty-five hundred years ago the great philosopher Aristotle, speaking of money, said that its value was determined by its quantity. If money is scarce, its value is high; if there is a superabundance of money, then it is cheap. The price of commodities, of course, varies conversely to the price of money; when money is dear commodity prices are low, and when money is cheap commodity prices are high. It seems that when one speaks of inflation a lot of timid people become frightened; the average man who is not familiar with the term visualizes a person going to a store with a wheelbarrow full of paper money with which to buy groceries. That is an absurd thought. I know something like that did happen in Germany some years ago, but when some of us in this section of the house suggest the issuing of more money we do not propose for a moment that it should be allowed to get out of control. I think perhaps when we speak of inflation we use the wrong term. The word frequently used by bankers and economists today is reflation. I do not know whether or not that is the proper word, but at any rate it indicates that the process of deflation of our currency has been carried to an extravagant degree. All that is asked by those who wish for a change is that it be Drought back to a reasonable level.
Let me give the simple illustration of milk. This commodity may be sold to the public watered to the extent of perhaps twenty-five per cent. I would call that inflated milk. It may be sold just as it comes from the cow; I would call that a proper standard. It may be dehydrated and sold as milk powder; I would call that a condition of deflation. That is the condition of our money today. It has been dehydrated, and we are only asking that it be hydrated or watered back to where it was a few years ago in [DOT]order to bring about a proper price level. The farmer, as well as the ordinary debtor, who contracted obligations three or four years ago finds himself compelled to pay back today about three hundred per cent of the actual debt, and we suggest that in carrying out this deflation or reflation it should be carefully managed.
After all, what have we in Canada today? A few days ago the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) told us that Canada had not been on the gold basis since 1929. As a matter of fact today we have a currency that is managed. The greatest of all the problems facing us in Canada today, it seems to me, and a problem common to the farmer as well as to the business man, is that of debts. The deflation during the last few years has tre-
mendously increased our debts, public as well as private. What are we facing? Today we are on the horns of a dilemma. One possibility is repudiation of those debts, and that is ngt confined entirely to private debts. If present conditions continue, hundreds of municipalities throughout Canada, and even some provinces, are almost sure to default in their payments in the months to come.
I say we are facing either a repudiation of debts or a reflation of currency to meet that condition. A year or two ago, when some of those in this section of the house suggested certain monetary changes, it was looked upon as bolshevism by some of our orthodox business men and newspapers, but today we find some of those same newspapers getting squarely behind those who advocate that policy. I hold in my hand a copy of the Toronto Saturday Night dated October 1. This is one of the most orthodox publications in Canada, which a few years ago would have poured scorn and ridicule upon any suggested change of this kind. On the front page I find a very excellent article on the money question by John Collingwood Reade. The very heading is arresting; it is:
Liquidation versus Repudiation
Post war conditions call for new financial machinery-Consumption of industry's products must be financed or debt repudiation will follow.
I do not wish to weary the house by quoting extensively from this article, but I do feel that it is worthy of some consideration. This article points out that in dealing with the situation prior to the deflation the United States had two courses open to it in connection with the European debt. They could have accepted goods, the product of European nations, in payment of those debts, or they could have forgiven the debts. There is no possibility of those debts ever being fully paid in gold, and those two courses are open to the United States today. In dealing with the former course, that of accepting goods in payment, the article points out that if the United States had decided to accept goods, those goods could have been distributed to the people of the United States without necessarily affecting their factories at all. It would have given them a larger percentage of goods; a greater quantity of goods would have been delivered to the individual, and the standard of living in the United States would have been increased immeasurably. It points out that a policy of that kind would necessitate certain monetary changes; if the extra amount of goods taken in payment of those debts had been balanced by an increase in currency, those goods could have been distributed to the people of the United States

Farm Relief-Mr. Campbell
without disturbing the business equilibrium of the world. In that case there would have been no depression.
I would ask you to call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

When the house rose
at six o'clock I was dealing with the money question and was referring to an article in the Toronto Saturday Night of October 1 last. Dealing with the question of how the United States might have collected their international debts, the article states:
It would be necessary for the American people to raise their standard by a very considerable amount if they are to be enabled to absorb the commodities tendered in payment of debt and still purchase the output of their own manufacturers.
The financial system, as at present constituted, is unable to finance the distribution of the enormous import of goods and services to which the existence of accrued debt entitles the American people without demoralizing the market for domestic output.
It goes on to say:
Repudiation is inevitable if one of the other alternatives is not adopted.
Then it says:
The proper manner of dealing with the world situation as it touches the maldistribution of equities and purchasing power is to institute a pragram of financial reorganization throughout the world such that the basis for money is provided by goods seeking a market, and that the necessity of competing for gold by bonusing exports is removed.
Then it comes to what I think is the allimportant part of the whole article. It states:
A superabundance of goods should be an advantage, not an embarrassment. If they are accompanied by the money with which to buy them they are an advantage.
The amendment which was moved by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) and which was ruled out of order, dealt with this very question and pointed out that in our opinion money should be based on the actual amount of goods to be distributed, because, after all, that is the only reason we need money-to distribute goods.
To come back to the article, it further states-and this is referring to Canada:
The fact is that we do not really need to borrow anything. In the last analysis, capital is an accumulation of labour, skill and resources. All four of these are already a drug on the Canadian market.
Farm Relief-Mr. Campbell

The concluding paragraph of the article sums up the situation in this way:
A new basis for the creation and distribution of money other than by gold accretions or the manufacture of new liabilities in exchange for bank credit can accomplish this, and it must be accompanied by a ready acceptance of goods so that it does not exhibit the evils of an uncontrolled inflation.
Again I would draw the attention of the house to the fact that this is not from a labour paper; it is not written by an ordinary theorist. It is on the front page of the Toronto Saturday Night.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODS WORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
speechtext:
I should like to take advantage of this opportunity to call the attention of the house to some conditions which in my judgment are not in the interests of the Canadian people.
The Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) seems to think that I always have a grievance. That may be so, but I would submit that it is not a personal grievance. If I had as my clients the Canadian bankers or the Canadian manufacturers or, we will say, the Canadian canners, perhaps I might find myself in a position in which I could give great praise to the government. But I have been trying to represent certain groups in this country which I consider under our system axe exploited groups. I wish I could truthfully say with one of the foremost leader of socialism in America, the late Eugene V. Debs:
While there is a lower class, I am in it. While there is a criminal element, I am of it. While there is a soul in prison, I am not free.
Or as James Russell Lowell expressed a somewhat similar thought a good many years ago:
If there breathe on earth a slave,
Are ye truly free and brave?
Is true freedom but to break Fetters for our own dear sake?
No! True freedom is to share
All the chains our brothers wear . . .

Again:
They are slaves who fear to speak
For the fallen and the weak;
They are slaves who diare not be
In the right with two or three.
So although, like most members of the house, I should like to have the commendation of the majority of the members, I feel that there are certain matters that I must speak of even if I may be criticized as merely a man with a grievance.
First of all, Mr. Speaker, may I venture to congratulate the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) upon the speech he made this afternoon. It seems to reveal a growing consciousness on his part of the seriousness of the problems now confronting us. My only wish would be that the spirit in which he delivered his speech could be more frequently manifested in this house, because it seems to me that beneath the party fight that occupies so much of our time there are aspirations and heart searchings on the part of a great many. I fancy conditions are rapidly becoming so serious it might well be that irrespective of party lines men are willing to give more serious attention to the real problems facing the people.
May I suggest that during the last few weeks of this session we have been witnessing a gradual curtailment of the rights of private members. This is a regular session, and yet the regular order of proceedings has been set aside. We have not had the opportunity of introducing private members' motions. Private members have had no opportunity to introduce bills, despite the fact that certain legislation was much needed. Further than that, the rules with regard to introducing a matter of urgent public importance have been so strictly interpreted that it has been almost impossible for us to introduce anything under that order. In that connection I refer to only one instance, namely that of the Sun Life management. True, there is a certain charge of criminal libel pending, but I submit that since the report of the superintendent of insurance has been tabled in the house, and since many of the figures which have been circulated to the public have been taken from that report, any hon. member should be allowed to discuss the management and the affairs of the Sun Life. I submit that a suit for libel has very little to do with the responsibility of this house towards the management of a great insurance company. Under the circumstances, all we can do is to point out that the government assumes heavy responsibility in refusing to allow public discussion

Unemployment-Mr. Woodsworth
of the affairs of a company in a position such as that occupied by the Sun Life.
Further than that, the trouble in our penitentiaries has received a great deal of public attention, and many of us would have liked to hear this matter discussed. We are told by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) that since there is a departmental investigation in progress it is unnecessary for us to have any further investigation until the departmental investigation has been completed. I submit that decision is not going to satisfy the 'public. Prisoners are the most helpless of people, because almost every man's mind is set against them. We have been taught to believe that criminals are anti-social and they are placed under such constraint that it is next to impossible for them to vent their grievances It seems to me, therefore, that owing to the fact they are, in a certain sense, wards of society, special protection should be thrown around them by a body such as this House of Commons, and if there is the slightest suspicion of unfair treatment or favoritism there should be the widest possible investigation by an impartial commission. I make these .statements merely in passing, because I do not wish to wait another two months before placing my views on record. It seems to me that the troubles in the penitentiaries offer the government a spendid opportunity to investigate not merely the administration of the penitentiaries, but also the whole matter of the treatment of criminals.
Again I point out that under ordinary circumstances a private member has two opportunities of bringing almost any matter before the house. One is afforded on the motion that the Speaker leave the chair for the house to resolve itself into committee of ways and means, and the other on the motion that the Speaker leave the chair for the house to go into committee of supply. The latter is the occasion upon which I am now speaking.
I repeat that owing to rulings of the chair it has been impossible for us to bring matters before the house in such a way as to obtain a full expression of the views of hon. members on any one question. Resolutions have been ruled out of order. We have been able to do only that which we are now doing, namely voice our protests. I cannot understand why a government would take that attitude, unless it is really afraid of the votes of its own supporters. That is the only reason which occurs to my mind. As I have said, I have come to the conclusion that by such rulings the rights' of private members are gradually being curtailed.
Another instance-we have been discussing matters of taxation. I shall not attempt to labour this point, but it does seem to me that when tariffs are arranged beforehand, and when they cannot be changed, the business of the house lacks reality. Another and perhaps more serious development which shows how far we are getting away from what most of us have thought to be a democratic form of government, lies in the fact that moneys have recently been loaned, without interest, to a private company. It would seem that repayment may be deferred almost indefinitely.
If that action can be taken by the government with regard to one corporation, I suggest it may be taken with regard to others, and it is hard to say just where such a practice may stop. An hon. member suggests we want some of that money. Yes, I do not see why the farmers or the labour men should not have help from the government, if private corporations can get it. Further than that, we must consider the guarantees which have been given to the banks. AVe have witnessed a very great extension of the principle of government by order in council. Indeed I am not quite sure whether sometimes orders in council were issued until considerable time had elapsed after certain gentleman's agreements had been given. Then, if our grain prices should not recover it is quite possible that the government may have committed itself to a policy which, a few years ago, was described as gambling in grain, and which may be very harmful to the financial structure of the country.
Further, according to the statement of the Prime Minister, Canada's foreign policy cannot be discussed while the situation is under review. That is a very serious matter, because the public generally ought to make its opinions felt before questions are finally decided.
Now I should like to come to the more immediate question of conditions among the unemployed in this country. I do not hesitate to take this opportunity, because I did not finish what I had to say on that matter a few evenings ago. With regard to certain charges which I had passed on to me about conditions in the camp at Riding Mountain, let me say this; both the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) and the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Murphy) read statements and correspondence which would seem to show that the conditions stated do not prevail. Personally I have not since then had the opportunity of investigating the matter. If they do not prevail, I am very glad. I would feel very sorry indeed that I read the letter, if

Unemployment-Mr. Woodsworth
the conditions stated do not prevail, but I read it in good faith, a letter from a man whom I have known and who I do not think was trying to deceive me. But if I made a mistake in judging him I am very sorry. I did not read it primarily in order to cast any reflection upon the management of the camps, but rather as an instance of the bad conditions under which a great many of our people are living at the present time. But whether or not one particular camp is bad or good, I submit that the government has not answered the statements we made in regard to the far-reaching nature of the prevailing unemployment, and the unsatisfactory policies that prevail with regard to the treatment of the unemployed. The minister advocates the back to the land movement. I agree that that may be a good thing as far as a few individuals are concerned, but after what we have heard from the prairies as to conditions on the land it is obvious that the back to the land movement is no solution of our general unemployment problem.
Further the Prime Minister announced that we are to have a conference to consider the question of unemployment insurance. As the house knows, I have advocated for a great many years, as have my colleagues, unemployment insurance, but frankly I think we have now almost passed the stage when it can be of any great value. With 800,000 unemployed, how can we possibly make provision for them under a contributory unemployment insurance scheme? They are outside of that scheme altogether. I cannot see how with the small numbers of men employed in industry to-day the necessary reserves can be built up. I shall be very glad indeed if some plan can be worked out between the dominion and the provinces under which a scheme of unemployment insurance can be put into operation. But again I say that is no solution of the problem that is going to face hundreds of thousands of our people during this coming winter.
I have no desire to delay the house, or I should have liked to offer a resolution something in these terms:
That all the words after "that" he struck out and the following substituted:
In the opinion of this house the government should take immediate action to provide for the unemployed either suitable work or adequate maintenance.
May I ask the hon. member a question? If the Dominion government will not assume any responsibility for unemployment insurance, what right have they to decide that it should be contributory?

Well, I think the
hon. member would have to ask that of the government. I presume that the announcement meant that the government would assume a certain share of responsibility if matters could be arranged between the governments. I hope it meant that, although I see that some of the papers came out with the announcement next day that the Prime Minister absolutely refused to consider unemployment insurance.
Mr. LaVERGNE :	Has the hon. gentleman those figures by provinces, that 800,000?

No; that was the
figure given by the Minister of Labour.
Mr. LaVERGNE: No, that was the number on relief.
Not all workmen.

No, that 800,000, as I understood the figures, included men, women and children. But I think there is no doubt whatever, according to the statistics given by my colleague from North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) and others, which I have checked carefully, that there are at least three quarters of a million unemployed at the present time.

Men, women and
children?

No, men and
women who would normally be engaged in work. Since the government has assumed the sole responsibility for dealing with this question, I said the other day that I thought about all we could do at this stage was to try to bring home to the house and to the government the real situation that exists among large numbers of our people.
I received a few weeks ago, from a United Church minister -who has a pastorate in one of the suburbs of Winnipeg, a letter from which I should like to read some extracts. He says:
The weather is still mild though there has been much snow and rain recently. We are glad because we do not have to get coal for a few days yet. There is no money in our house but 75 cents in my purse. The secretary of the church has about $50 he got from the ladies' aid a week or so ago. Some of it is needed to buy coal for the church as the company would give us no more on credit. Our bill for last year is still unpaid. I mean the church bill.
I am in debt, the church is in debt, and a great many of my people are on relief. Those not on relief have been so reduced that they have little more than an existence. The weather has been wet, cloudy and cold and I have often looked at the men working in the ditches here near the church with pity. The outlook for so many of them seems so hopeless. I wonder if

Unemployment-Mr. Woodsworth
a great many of them really realize except in a dim way what is happening. A day or two ago on a cold morning preceding a storm of rain and snow about twenty men came to the corner nearest our house to dig a ditch alongside of the road. A fence and tall residence and the church building gave some protection from the north wind. Half of the men at any time were huddled against this fence. You see they are not clothed for this weather and work and they have no spirit to try to keep up heat by working. This work on the roads and ditches is a most wasteful kind of expenditure. So many, many men accomplishing so little. Working three days a week for "relief tickets" and idling most of the time.
Further on he speaks of general conditions.
The school board have sent out a letter to the parents of boys and girls to say that if the fee of $2 per month is not forthcoming from all able to pay that the high school will be closed in the near future. I understand that the fee is not coming in, so we anticipate the worst. This high school has been going about twenty years and does good work. If closed five teachers will be out of a job. I have a boy in grade II, a bright youth, and I do not know just what we shall do.
A movement is afoot to establish some kind of municipal store in town to supply groceries to the unemployed. The merchants don't like this and are protesting.
Again:
The mounties have been very busy rounding up the transients here east of town and at the Canadian Pacific Railway north of here. Motorcycles are constantly on the run. People despise these men. The children call names at them as they pass on the streets and say "Take the yellow off your legs and put it down your backs." One cold night 66 men were turned over to the local police here. The man on duty is a kind fellow and got them some warm floors to sleep on.-except four of them. These had stopped and sat down on the sidewalk apart from the main body. Ten minutes later the policeman found them all four asleep there.
In the face of that about all we can get from the Minister of Labour is that no one need suffer. But these men are suffering. The minister who writes me this letter goes on to give me some individual cases:
Two of the men in the gang referred to were mechanics in the shops. Both about 29 years old. married, with children. They had started with the company at 16 years and never had done any work except at the machinists' bench.
Another man-

Then he and the family went to the lake where he has a small cottage, and spent the summer. It was cheap living because he has a pass and could come up every few days for groceries. Now he is back with his father-inlaw and on "relief." A week ago on Monday when out to talk with the men in the ditch- a common practice of mine-I met Ed. He told
