speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I think the
hon. member should either give the name or take personal responsibility for the facts stated.

I am quite willing to take responsibility for the statements I have read. It seems very strange that with these conditions prevalent the Prime Minister can have the effrontery to quote scripture. He says, "The poor ye have always with you,'' as though the Man of Nazareth could be possibly conceived as condoning our indifference to the welfare of our fellow men. Since the Prime Minister has set the precedent perhaps I might take the liberty of quoting a passage or two of scripture:
Woe unto you also, ye lawyers!
The reference, of course, is to ecclesiastical lawyers, but since the Prime Minister has undertaken to interpret scripture perhaps he might be included in that class.
Woe unto you also, ye lawyers! for ye lade men with burdens grievous to be borne, and ye yourselves touch not the burdens with one of your fingers.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
What about the false
prophets?

Yes, there is also a good deal to be said about false prophets. If

the hon. gentleman cares to know it, the author of that last passage is Luke. May I quote the next passage, in all seriousness:
For I was an hungred, and ye gave me no meat; I was thirsty, and ye gave me no drink; I was a stranger, and ye took me not in; naked, and ye clothed me not; sick, and in prison, and ye visited me not. . . . Inasmuch as ye did it not to one of these least, ye did it not to me.
How about the next part?

There are certain
gentlemen who think this is a matter for great levity. I think it is a time for common sense. I believe it is time to consider the very foundations of this civilization which we commonly call Christian. There are those who seem to think that any discussion of actual existing affairs is an attempt to wreck our civilization, I venture to say that it is the only possible way in which we can save our civilization. Before now I have quoted in this house that old favourite passage from James Russell Lowell, which I venture to quote again tonight:
. . . Think ye that building shall endure
Which shelters the noble and crushes the poor?
Oh, oh.

You think that
may be met with derision? Very well. I am firmly convinced, Mr. Speaker, that it is quite within the range of possibility that if this thing goes on very much longer a great many of us will suffer very greatly indeed because of the fact that we have neglected those in our community who today are suffering. I wish hon. gentlemen opposite could understand that I am not merely censuring one government or another. I wish they could understand that tonight I am not thinking so much in terms of politics as I am in terms of the needs of these people. Hon. gentlemen do not seem able to comprehend that point of view. I urge that we each have our responsibility. There is not one of us who would be sleeping in as good a bed, or eating as good food, or going on with our business as easily as we do, if we took seriously some of these ethical teachings which I have ventured to quote in the house tonight. I think the time is coming when if we refuse to do these things because of higher motives we shall be forced to do them because of the effect of the economic laws which are working out a new type of life.
Who has refused them?

An hon. gentleman asks: "Who has refused them?" I say

Unemployment-Mr. Woodsworth
the fact is that there are hundreds of thousands of people who are not able to live a decent, normal life. We ask parliament to take some responsibility in this matter.
They are taking it.

Some one speaking on behalf of the government says that the government are taking responsibility. They are, in form, taking responsibility, and I would not say a word in reproach if they were meeting fully the needs, but in my judgment the measures that they have adopted are not meeting the needs. To be perfectly frank, I doubt very much whether under the existing competitive system they can meet the needs. That is why some of us look forward to a radical and complete change in our whole economic system. However, I take it for granted for the moment that the present economic system is equal to meeting the needs. This seems to be the prevalent impression in the house. On that ground I charge that our present policies are not meeting the needs.
The needs of the people should have prior consideration. You may call that mere demagogy, if 3'ou like, but, as I have said ever since I entered public life, when the profits of shareholders or the interests of big business come into conflict with the needs of men, women and children, then I have urged that the needs of men, women and children should have priority. I know that is considered to be a very extreme doctrine, but I firmly believe in it.

Everybody believes in
it.

We are not putting it into practice. If we were we would not have hundreds of our young people walking the street without any chance of continuing their education, some of them not knowing where the next meal is to come from; we would not have thousands of people in the jungles as we have today, herded together under conditions not even sanitary, and wholly unsatisfactory from the point of view of the standards of good citizenship; we would not have the riots such as have occurred during the last few weeks in a number of our western cities. These men who have been rioting, or the majority of them, were until a few years ago good workmen. If we go on in this way it will not be very long before their spirit will be broken and we shall have a large group of unemployable people and a considerable number of criminals. I may be right or I may be wrong, but if I
think that way, surely I am under an obligation to state my thoughts as forcibly as I can.
The other day the Prime Minister took the standpoint of property and property rights, and I feel it requires some hammering to get the other point of view effectively before the public. He said:
We believe that the honest efforts of man should be rewarded. Since when has it become a crime to acquire property? The initiative of genius should be rewarded.
That is his defence of our present economic arrangements, but I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that the ordinary citizen is not having his honest efforts rewarded; he is not having a chance these days even to work. He has taken his full share in the building up of this country, he has worked upon our railroads, in our lumber camps and in our mines; he has done his fair share of the hard work, and yet when we reach a depression he is laid aside and has no chance of receiving a reward for his honest efforts. The Prime Minister asked: "Since when has it become a crime to acquire property?'' My submission is that the vast majority of the people on relief, and many more in a desperate condition of anxiety, have no chance of acquiring property. Indeed they have been forced to watch their homes slip away from them; they have had no chance to keep even the little property they have acquired. Why should it be right for a wealthy man to be protected by the government in his possession of property while the poor man receives no assistance, or very little, when his property is in danger? It is all very well to talk about the initiative of genius being rewarded, but let me point out to the house that there are hundreds of young people today who have no opportunity to develop their initiative.
I was talking with a conductor the other day and he told me that he wished I could find some job for his girl. He said that she had been trained as a school teacher, that he had given her the best chance possible, but now she was at home and if she remained there much longer she would become absolutely discouraged. He said that as long as he had a roof over his head she would not suffer hunger. The position of this girl is that of thousands of other young people who have been prepared to enter the professions. Many, though, have not the shelter of a parental roof.
I think of a young man in my home city whom I met only a few weeks ago. Two years ago he graduated from a university in civil engineering. He had always been willing to

Unemployment-Mr. Woodsworth
undertake any kind of work; as a matter of fact he had gone out to do unskilled labour in a foundry, but the depression having become more severe he was turned out of even that job. His father had worked hard for many years to give him a chance at a college education. The father was a poor workingman and could not afford to support his son in idleness, and this boy had drifted around doing casual jobs, even thinking of whether or not he should commit suicide. At a matter of fact the only thing that saved him was a chance to get a position in Camp Borden which lasted two or three months. That offered relief for the time being and he took it because it tided him over until the spring time. He told me that almost the entire membership of his graduating class were in a similar position to that in which he found himself. If we really believed that the interests of the people should take priority over property rights, then we would immediately take such steps as would provide the unemployed either with suitable work or with adequate maintenance.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. A. GORDON (Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall endeavour to make my remarks very brief. During the course of this session I have covered in the main some of the activities of the various governments throughout Canada directed toward taking care of the situation which exists in our country, and I have spread upon the record, in so far as the departments of government can collect information, the situation with which this government is endeavouring so earnestly to cope. I have listened to the addresses made in the house, and while I do not think we should complain about the descriptive phrases and at times almost extreme language which has been used, it has occurred to me very frequently that perhaps the addresses would have been more effective and more helpful if hon. members had taken the trouble to inquire from the departments of government and thus get a more complete picture of the situation as reflected in dependable governmental sources, rather than base their remarks upon fragmentary information as disclosed in letters and newspaper clippings which have been so frequently resorted to.
I was considerably disappointed when I listened to the criticism of the hon. member for North Battleford (Mr. McIntosh), and I believe also the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer), in connection with the administration of the lands owned in part by the soldier settlement board. As the house knows, a complete reorganization of that department was effected some eighteen months ago. I say

with a great deal of confidence that the reorganized force of that department is very efficient and is carrying on its work in a manner that, I believe, commends itself to the great majority of the settlers under its control.
The hon. member for North Battleford made some startling statements, statements that distressed me greatly, wiith respect to two or three settlers in his locality and with regard to the efforts made by the Saskatchewan government, with a contribution from this government, toward returning to the land people who had previously had agricultural experience, who expressed a desire to return to the land and who were then receiving direct relief in the cities. My mind, however, was relieved and my anxiety in large measure dispelled when I found, after the interrogation of the hon. member for North Battleford by the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion), that the hon. member for North Battleford, having made those statements, in order to prove them and to hammer them home in the way that probably only he could do, proceeded to read from a newspaper, owned and edited by him, a report made on the cases by himself. During my business life I have had some acquaintance with the proper method of proving a case, and if his method is a proper one, then I suggest to the hon. member for North Battleford that I would not have a .chance at all against such an argument as he advanced. Can anyone imagine a man standing in the House of Commons, criticizing what I believe to be a very efficient department of government, a department that is doing a great work in Canada, and particularly at a time like this, making charges such as he made, and then attempting to prove them by reading his own report in his own newspaper? I can say only that my anxiety in the matter was at once dispelled. In order that the house may not labour under any misapprehension with respect to the attitude of the department in regard to not only the soldier settlers but all the settlers under the jurisdiction of the soldier settlement board, let me say that since this government came into power, of more than 20,000 settlers on lands in part owned by the government-and I say that because the settlers have an equity in those lands-in respect of only three-tenths of one per cent have the government felt they should take some action in order to protect the equity of the crown in their holdings.
Just one word more with respect to the situation at Lloydminster referred to by the hon. member. An organization was formed there among the soldier settlers; they com-

Unemployment-Mr. Gordon
munieated with me and they sent out rather an alarming circular as to what attitude they intended to adopt with respect to discharging their obligations to the crown. But when they met, there apparently was sound sense among most of the settlers, and those who organized the union were not able to put across the sentiments expressed in the circular. We received from this union a repont of the meeting, and the suggestions in it are almost identical with the policy that has been followed by the soldier settlement board since this government came into power. The director of soldier settlement is constantly moving from coast to coast interviewing the field staff in connection with the work, and with reference to the oustanding case brought forward by the hon. member for North Battle-ford, the director instructed his field superintendent at Edmonton to go down at once to that locality and investigate it. Whom does the house suppose he took with him? None other than the hon. member for North Battleford. The superintendent took him right down to that settler and let him investigate the condition for himself. He knew the arrangement at that time and after seeing the condition for himself, he drove home with the superintendent and did not have a single word [DOT] of criticism to offer. Yet he spreads that story upon the record here for the edification of hon. members, which record read by the uninformed would, if not contradicted, do great injury to the work being carried on by this department.
Within the time allotted to me it would be utterly impossible to cover the various criticisms of the government that have been made from the other side of the house. The colonization at home scheme that I in my innocence thought would meet with the approval of the people of this country does not seem to commend itself to some hon. members on the other side. I have listened to speeches by some western members and I know from my own knowledge that certain of the pronouncements made in this chamber by a number of representatives of western Canada-not all of them by any means-have resulted in those who heretofore had confidence in the financial stability of the western provinces, withdrawing their support from them, selling the bonds of those provinces and investing the proceeds in other securities. I put it to those members from western Canada who day in and day out seem to take a great delight in condemning their own provincial governments, condemning their own country, condemning the people in it-because painting pictures such as they paint is the worst sort of condemnation they can offer of 53719-104
their own community and province: Can they go home to their people and be happy in the thought that they have stood up in this chamber and spread upon the record a picture of conditions in their own part of the country calculated only to condemn it in the eyes of anyone outside those provinces? I offer the suggestion that that sort of thing should stop. I am not unacquainted with western Canada. I was in the west for a considerable period of time, long before the arrival there of some of the hon. members who have talked so earnestly, or at least so loudly, about conditions in those provinces, and I still have many acquaintances throughout that part of Canada. I do not hold any such views of western Canada as do those members. I think I can go out there now and meet many thousands of farmers who of course are not getting the prices we would like to see them get for their produce. That is most lamentable, and it is something everyone in the house, I am sure, will do everything possible to try to correct. But I know thousands upon thousands of western farmers are absolutely firm in their belief that by accepting this temporary condition, and by exhibiting that courage which they in common with the other peoples of Canada so abundantly possess, they will overcome the present depression, and western Canada will again be prosperous and rightfully styled the golden west.
We have heard what perhaps I might call strange doctrines preached at this time, but that is nothing new in the history of the world. Anyone who has taken the time and had the opportunity to review the past must have found that the great writers of those days wrote just as learnedly about the difficulties besetting the world then as the writers of to-day. Times of general depression always bring into bold relief new corrective ideas, and at times permit people to offer as a corrective an extremity of view to which in my humble opinion we should not give too much heed, because in any situation extremity of view and extravagance of statement are not helpful.
We find some people, for instance, suggesting that there should ibe shorter hours of labour, by which they claim labour would be better distributed. I am not going to quarrel seriously with that. I would not mind myself if some of the duties I am trying to discharge were divided up and someone else shouldered some of them for a while. I think it is fair to say that if it were possible to cut down the hours of labour and divide up the work to the point where labour sufficient to keep a man's body and mind in good condition were available it would probably be a good thing

Unemployment-Mr. Gordon

But on the one hand we are highly industrialized and on the other, an agricultural country and a producer of raw products. There are other countries just as highly industrialized as Ours which we have to meet in competition in the markets of the world. If it is still to maintain its standard of living, what possible chance has Canada, acting alone in reducing the hours of labour, of competing in the markets of the world with the manufacturers of other countries? The thing is so simple that it does not admit of argument The situation was very well put in the British House of Commons on the 20th of October last by Sir Henry Batterton the Minister of Labour, where he said:
Experience shows that an international convention regulating hours of labour will not be ratified by the countries which are industrially important unless it can be so framed as to make provision for the veTy real difficulties that must be encountered in its practical application. His Majesty's government, therefore, while favouring a full examination of the problem of reducing hours of work without reducing the standard of living of the wage-earning population, have opposed and will continue to oppose any attempt to improvise a convention which evades the difficulties instead of solving them. Such a convention will be of no effect save to cause friction and misunderstanding and to delay the solution of the problem with which it professes to deal.
If by international action such a thing could be brought about, I do not think there is a shadow of doubt that this government and this country would be found supporting it.
It has also been suggested-and I listened very carefully to the addresses made on this subject-that we should inflate our currency. I am not going to offer much on that subject, because frankly I feel that while I can build up a theory on both sides I am not sure that either of them is sound. Quotations from almost every known writer on economics have been read in this house, but I believe I am sufficiently well acquainted with the writers on economic subjects and their works to say that I could take a dozen of the foremost authorities on the subject and find half a dozen on the one side and half a dozen on the other. I have no doubt that in the other legislative halls of the world the pronouncements on this subject dealt with by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) are being proclaimed with a solemnity which ought to carry weight in those chambers. I know this, that there are many things that might be said in favour of the view which has been put forward. At the moment we do not think it desirable-I am speaking of the government- to inflate the currency of this country.
The hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler), who gave such an interesting address
IMr. Gordon.]
this afternoon, with his usual skill and care suggested-I took his words down and I noticed the flirtatious look that he gave to his left when he said it-
Order. I would ask, Mr. Speaker, whether that is parliamentary language.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: He said that there should be a reasonable and controlled degree of inflation. That is a very subtle description. I suggest to the hon. member that I would almost be able to subscribe to it if he would leave out the word "controlled." If my experience in business means anything, just start to give anything away and let the impression go abroad that the well will never run dry, and you will have a great deal of difficulty in controlling the importunings of those who would seek to dip into it.
Does my hon. friend suggest that it should be uncontrolled?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Not at all.
I was wondering if the minister was speaking out of his experience with reference to the blank cheque.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
I congratulate the right hon. gentleman for his very valuable contribution to the debate,
I have listened to another great grievance which has been commented upon from time to time in reference to the great corporations of this country-private corporations, but still great-which from time to time split their stock and probably get an authorized increase in their capaitalization. I am sure I made reference to what my idea of such a thing was when I presented to the house the report of the investigation into the Beau-ha,mois project. In substance I said then that every dollar added to the capital cost of the development of any industry or national resource meant that the product of that industry or resource would be increased in cost to the consumer to the extent of the interest required to carry that additional charge, and my remarks brought forth a certain amount of applause from those who sit to the furthest left of the Speaker. Now I offer this as a suggestion. I hear from many members opposite about the iniquity of watered stock in private corporations, and I am in thorough agreement with those who advance the argument respecting watered stock. But, I ask, what is the difference in principle between private corporations watering their stock and the country watering its currency? Hon. members who would condemn the private corporation will commend the government

Unemployment-Mr. Gordon
for doing the same thing in principle. They are willing to approbate and reprobate in the same breadth. I may be wrong, but I can see no difference in principle.
The hon. gentleman is quite wrong in his interpretation of what other people are discussing.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Perhaps I am. Then, there is a class of people in Canada concerning which no mention has been made, so far as I know, by any of the speakers who at this time have condemned the government's action. I have reference to the type of man who is shouldering great responsibilities in providing for his wife and family, the man who, unlike many others who during the past ten years attempted to hitch his bronco to the financial cart for the wildest ride in history, has often denied himself the necessities of life in order that he might set aside a fund in the form of government bonds, an annuity or otherwise to provide for his old age or against misadventure or death in the interests of those for whom he may be responsible. There are many people in Canada such as I have described, but I have not heard one word about them. A number of members are flirting with ideas which have been projected, but with which I did not think they would be in entire accord. I venture to hazard the opinion that when the class of persons to which I have referred read of the advanced socialization suggested by some hon. members, and hear of the state undertaking to provide this, that and the other thing, they will wonder: "What was the use of it all? Why should I have tried to live a disciplined life? Why should I have tried to scrape and save to provide against the future and to give my family a fair chance to get along in life?" Those are the people who have not had consideration in this chamber, and I think it is high time they had. We should have at least some consideration for people of that type.
What is the difference between one who has put his savings into government bonds and one who has invested in a farm?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
The government has been earnestly endeavouring to see that those who require relief are given it. I should like very shortly to spread on the record what the government has endeavoured to do since this situation developed. I do not wish to dwell upon the facts, but would begin by saying that undoubtedly Saskatchewan has had a very difficult time. There was a time when 53719-104^
this government, because of successive crop failures in that province, was providing sustenance for upwards of 300,000 people. There was no hesitancy about dealing with that situation. The government, realizing its responsibility, took hold of it promptly and spent huge sums of money, because such expenditures were necessary in order that those living in the stricken areas would have a chance either to move somewhere else or to try again. This government did not hesitate to accept its burden and to endeavour to discharge what it considered to be its responsibility.
The complaint has been made and this government has been condemned because in the province of Saskatchewan notes were taken for relief. In the first place, let me say that the federal government had nothing to do with the matter; but I should like to add that I am not condemning the Saskatchewan relief commission for its action, for the very obvious reason that the people they were helping were not indigents, in the true sense of the word the people who were the victims of thal great tragedy are sturdy, wholesome, courageous Canadians, people who are not accustomed to taking money from governments, or from anybody else, without repaying. I cannot tell how many, but at least a great many of them said, "Here are our notes; we will pay you this money back." In face of that, what could the Saskatchewan relief commission do? Although reports are not available, I am told that many of those people are already making provision for retirement of advances. I can see nothing in that transaction concerning which the Saskatchewan relief commission, the government of that province or this government, should be condemned.
Throughout Canada appeals were made to this government the substance of which were: that the depression was general, and that it had cast a great burden upon the provinces- not such a burden, I suggest, as would take it out of the ordinary rule that provinces and municipalities have a primary responsibility; but there was such a general need that this government felt, and I think properly, that they should contribute to the provinces according to the need. What has the government done? In the four western provinces, either by way of direct non-recoverable advances or in recoverable loans, the Dominion government has supplied the sum of $73,844,130.98. And this very day, when the government was being condemned by the hon. member for Willow Bunch,, in a speech that was

Unemployment-Mr. Gordon
delivered in perhaps as extravagant a style as I ever listened to, the province in which he lives is asking for further assistance in financing its affairs, and its application is under consideration by this government.
He voted against it.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
For all of Canada this government has provided the sum $115,631,733.80 mp to date for the purpose of tiding the provinces, the municipalities and the people generally over this trying period. That money does not come from people who have not got it. The tribute must be levied upon every Canadian citizen. It is those who have who will contribute that money, not those who have not. And I suggest to those who would criticize that that is no mean contribution; that this government might easily be criticized for having pledged the credit of the state in too large an amount. But as far as the government is concerned it is ready to meet any criticism of that sort.
I could enlarge upon this picture and give the details of how this money was distributed. We know from reports that come in weekly from sources throughout Canada that the giving of this help to the provinces, to the municipalities, and through them to the individual, has not created, as was suggested by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), the fear that the people will not know where their next meal is coming from. Not at all. Because as far as this government is concerned, as I have before stated in this house, we will continue to see that the people of this country will not suffer for fuel and food and the necessities of life. And while we are doing it I suggest to all hon. members of this house, regardless of their political persuasion, that when they go home and meet conditions that are perhaps not as they would like them to be, they should not be content to say to their constituents:	"If you are not getting along very
well, blame it on those terrible Tories!" That is not helpful. Let every hon. member go to his constituency as a Canadian, as a lover of his fellow man, as a lover of his country, and say to his people:	"The government, the
state, is assuming a tremendous responsibility. The state is willing to continue to assume it, but you as an individual have a duty to perform to yourself, to your family, to your community, to your country. Do not lose the opportunity; do anything you can to help, because individual effort will help probably more than any other effort that can be put forth. That is the right attitude, the attitude which ultimately will prevail in this
	.
country, in spite of the speeches that we have listened to. I have been through Canada perhaps as thoroughly as any member of this house. I have had to do with its economic complexities from many angles. I know the people of Canada, and I know that they are well aware of the opportunities that are here. But this dislocation of world affairs came down in the year 1929 so rapidly and with such compelling force that even those in the highest places in finance, in industry, in all the various vocations of life, were totally unable to conceive of the immensity of the problem that they would shortly have to face.
I did not intend to take even this much time, but I say in conclusion: Go out from this chamber as Canadians; do not be content to say as partisans that the government has failed, but carry the message to the Canadian people that all is not lost by any means; that we have a great country, and a small population; that we have wonderful assets, tremendous resources for the people to make use of. As far as this government is concerned it will put forth every effort, yes, it will go to its last available dollar to see that those who are unable to take advantage of those opportunities will not suffer during this coming winter.

May I ask a question? I
understood the minister to say that some farmers were willing to do without in order that they might come through. Would he be kind enough to suggest what he thinks the farmer should do without in order to come through?

All I can say is that the
amount was approved by the Clerk of the House in the ordinary course and submitted

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes. I have not the
accounts before me, but I must point out to my hon. friend that the account was incurred by a committee of this house, not by the government. I could get the account for my hon. friend if he would like to see it.
I do not think for a moment that when the committee authorized the employment of these gentlemen they had any conception that it would cost any such amount.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I may say that like the
hon. gentleman I thought the amount was very large. But they were instructed by the committee to do the work. The charges were tariff charges. We did not ask that the account be taxed, because you cannot tax it, but we asked that it be moderated. However, the account is here as it stands, and they have complained bitterly that it has not been paid. We have no money with which to pay it without the vote of the house, and that is why it is here.

I would suggest, then, that
we do not pass this item and ask them to wait until the spring. They would have had to wait in any case but for this special session.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
They thought provision
had been made last session, though as a matter of fact it had not.

I recall when this account
was presented to the committee. What the Prime Minister has said is quite correct. We went into the items and discovered that instead of the account being greater than was customary for such a company, they had given us a very material reduction because of the depression. Of course I objected to the charges myself; I thought they were much more than I would be able to earn in an hour or two, but that was their charge and we could not get any further.

This account is for the
work of auditors we had looking into the question of gasoline. These men were sent out by the committee; first they went to the
British American and the MoColl-Frontenac companies, where they spent five or six days. Later they were sent to Sarnia and Halifax to investigate certain definite points for the committee, concerning the price of crude oil, the amount of crude oil taken by the various refineries, the amount of gasoline obtained from the oil, and the prices of the gasoline and of the oil. They spent a good deal of time there and when they came back to the committee we asked them what they had found with regard to the British American and McColl-Frontenac Company. They told us they had found nothing and that they had no report to make, but said they would go back again if the committee wished. I think anyone looking up the records of that inquiry will find that the auditors said they had no report to make in connection with the McColl-Frontenac and Imperial Oil companies. If two experts had been sent out by Imperial Oil to justify a higher price for gasoline they could not have found two men who could have done the work better. These men reported that the Imperial Oil Company were not charging too much; that they were making a profit of only one cent a gallon, and that the price of gasoline in Canada was due to the bootlegging of gasoline from the United States, though I do not know where they got that information. At that time the committee said, "We do not want that sort of information; we want the facts and figures in order to draw our own conclusions." As a matter of fact the auditors brought in their conclusions without the actual figures. After arguing with them for a whole day we did manage to obtain a few figures, and they told us that if we wanted the other information they could figure it out but they did not have it prepared. So far as the committee was concerned the work done by those men was very unsatisfactory, though no doubt it was satisfactory to Imperial Oil and the other companies in general.
A minority report was brought in following that inquiry. The price of gasoline is disturbing the people from one end of Canada to the other; in fact it is disturbing people the world over. The price of gasoline in the world has followed the price of wheat, of coffee, of cotton and of many other things. Standard Oil of New Jersey has been looked upon as the tool of John D. Rockefeller, and for years the people of the United States have tried to pass legislation curtailing its activities and profits. They were not successful, but in 1929 or 1930 mother nature took a hand and more crude oil was produced than the world could consume. Consequently in 1930 or 1931 the price of gasoline fell all over
Sttppl y-Le gelation

the world, and continued to fall until crude oil was selling in Oklahoma and Texas, the mid-continent field, for ten cents a barrel. In Canada, however, the price of gasoline was maintained1; this is the only country in the world where the price remained high. It was kept up by the tariff and dumping duty imposed by this government. Last year, however, when the United States found that too much crude oil was being produced, they began to curtail production. They said, "We will cut down production and increase the price," and this did work to a certain extent. Finally they woke up and found this to be a world condition, so they called together the oil producers of the world with the idea of cutting down production all over the world in order to keep up prices. Many of these oil producers would not enter into a combine of that kind, with the result that the world price for oil remained1 low. We find now that the United States are asking for a duty against outside gasoline in order to increase the price in that country.
The government kept up the price of gasoline in Canada by four or five cents a gallon, which made it possible for Imperial Oil to declare a profit of over $17,000,000 last year. Standard Oil of New Jersey owns some sixty-nine per cent of the shares of Imperial Oil of Canada, and that company received some $12,700,000 in profits from the Canadian company. In other words, though they suffered a loss of $4,000,000 on all their operations, Standard Oil of New Jersey were able to declare a profit of $8,000,000; they took $12,700,000 from our Canadian consumers in order to do so. I think it is time we in Canada showed a little of that red blood about which the Minister of Railways spoke, and stopped being cheque signers and dividend payers for our American cousins.
At the time the committe was sitting the Bhell Oil Company was bringing in gasoline at four and a fraction cents a gallon at Montreal. They were selling that gasoline wholesale, in tank car lots, for something like 12 cents a gallon. I had a private individual in Ottawa go to the Department of National Revenue to inquire what dumping duty would be put on gasoline coming from Roumania, but we could not get any information. They said: "We will have to find out what their money is worth and what is the exchange rate before we can tell you what the charge will be." The result was that nobody attempted to bring in gasoline from any other part of the world for fear of the exchange being so high that they would not be able to make a profit.
I Mr. Donnelly.]
Not long ago the government saw fit to take off the dump duty on gasoline, but at the same time they passed orders in council stating that gasoline brought in from the United States by an ordinary consumer would have to pay the wholsesale price there plus the excise tax of one cent per gallon on the American gallon, equal to one and a quarter cents on the Canadian gallon. When I asked the Minister of National Revenue about this he said that no orders in council had been passed, that this was something done by the Liberal government. It is true that the Liberal government did pass legislation which fixed a fair market value at whatever the price was in the country of origin, but why did this government pass orders in council stating that the value for duty purposes would be the wholesale price at the refinery plus the American excise tax of one cent per gallon? I understand that American refiners do not pay that one cent tax when gasoline is exported, but the government has said that if the consumer brings in gasoline he must pay the wholesale price, plus that one cent tax. If he cannot make the American refiner take that tax, it must be paid to the customs. This means a one and a quarter cent protection for the oil refineries in the Dominion of Canada. In fact, when added to the other charges, this protection amounts to from one and three quarter cents to two cents per gallon. Our oil companies are enjoying this protection in addition to the regular duty of two and a half cents per gallon. I asked the minister why orders in council were passed providing that the refiners would not have to take into account this one cent excise tax, and he said that no such order was passed. The supplement to appraisers' bulletin number 3897, reads as follows:
On importations of gasoline to be used bona fide for blending purposes and not for resale as a motor fuel in the condition as imported, the excise tax should not be included in the fair market value for regular or special duty purposes.
Why did the government make that exception with regard to refiners or blenders? Why did they insist that the Canadian consumer who brings in gasoline must pay the one cent excise tax? I submit that this was done in the hope that additional protection would be given to the refineries and the Canadian public would not be the wiser.

The hon. member who has just spoken (Mr. Donnelly) said something about the report itself not being satisfactory, but I shall not attack it upon that ground. These accountants were entitled to make their

Supply-Legisla t ion
own report but it may well be considered uunsatisfaotory on the ground that they were asked to obtain certain information which it would seem they did not obtain. I followed the proceedings of this committee very closely, and that is the conclusion I have come to: all they brought back was a whitewashing report which they were not asked for. A large portion of the accountant's report was included bodily in the report of the committee.
I have in my hand a copy of what I assume the Minister of Finance was alluding to when he said he had an itemized account. This account would seem to cover the services not of a man, an individual or a firm, but of a whole army. We have the whole bunch here with the excepution perhaps of the furnace man-there is no amount low enough to cover the services of such a man. The first item is for the principal, 58 days and 3 hours ait $50 per day, total $2,921.43. Luckily there was only one principal. The next item is for supervisor, 73 days and 2 hours at $35 per day, total $2,565. I am speaking only from memory, but I believe there were some twenty days upon which the committee sat. Of course these men would be working when the committee was not sitting, but seventy-three working days would represent over two months and a half. The itemized account states that the charges are for a seven hour diay, and it might be possible that in their integrity and industry these men worked fourteen hours per day. Otherwise I cannot see how they could have worked two and one-half months during the time the committee was sitting. Then we come to first assistants. Apparently there were a number of these, because the account is for 123 days at $25 per day. Then there are second assistants, 43 days at $20 per day; third assistants at $15 per day, and fourth assistants at $10 per day. Unfortunately we did not have many fourth assistants; the account is only for 14 days. The total account amounts to $9,756.46. In addition to this there are out-of-pocket expenses totalling $1,477, but if there -are vouchers to cover this amount, I cannot object. The hon. member to my left mentioned something about a price cut owing to the depression buit I hate to think what this account would have been if there had not been a depression.
Either the Minister of Finance or the Prime Minister stated that these rates were according to the recognized scale for professional accountants. Thait is quite interesting, but there is also a recognized scale for doctors and lawyers. Jf you happen to be dissatisfied with
either your lawyer's or doctor's bill and try to dispute it, the first lawyer or doctor to whom you go will tell you that you have not been charged much more than half what you could have been charged under the schedule. When a doctor charges you $2.50 or $5 per visit, you will find that his schedule calls for a charge five times that. These schedules are arranged by these close corporations but they are never enforced, and that fact is to the credit of both the lawyers and the doctors.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No bargain was made antecedent to the employment -being given to this firm. They have rendered an account which was referred to me personally and I could find no way by which it could be reduced. If we do not pass it we will be compelled to grant a fiat and they will recover the money in a court of law.

If that is the case, there is no use in my wasting the time of the committee. At the same time, it is a good thing to uncover these things as they can -be remembered the next time we need the services of accountants.

Item agreed to.
Pensions-Pensions to families of members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police who lost their lives while on duty-further amount required-
To provide for a pension to Mrs. Catharine Mildred Ralls, equal to one-half of her late husband's daily regimental pay and ration allowance, from July 6, 1932, to March 31, 1933, $497.65.
To provide compassionate allowances to Victor. Everett, Doreen and Stanley Ralls, at $30 per annum each, from July 6, 1932, to March 31. 1933, $88.43.

I should like to direct the attention of the minister to a case which I consider to -be very conservative. I -brought this to his attention this afternoon by presenting the particulars to his private secretary, but I think I might be .permitted just one moment to state the facts of the case I have in mind. This is a veteran of the South African and Flanders wars. He was gassed but was not considered as pensionable. After discharge he was confined to hospital; and the authorities, after investigating his case, undertook to defray his hospital expenses and granted him a compassionate allowance of $20 per month. The point I desire to raise is that this $20 per month has been withdrawn. The communication which I received and which I passed on to the minister was from the president of the Lacombe board of trade, a man who I believe is thoroughly acquainted with the veteran and in whom I have the utmost confidence. I do not know this particular returned soldier; I -am relying entirely
Supply-Mail Subsidies

upon the evidence of the doctors and also the plea made by the president of the board of trade of the town of Lacoim.be. I merely wish to urge that the Minister of Pensions reconsider the withdrawal of that compassionate allowance. The man in question is suffering from cancer and I do not think he can last very long. He is unable to work and has no other resources. I do not know whether the minister is listening to me or not, but I hope he will reconsider the discontinuance of that compassionate allowance.

Item agreed to.
Mail subsidies and steamship subventions- British Columbia and Australia and/or China, services between-further amount required, $35,000.
To what companies is this subvention going?

The British Canadian
Steamship Company, Limited. The contract is dated August 15, 1932. It was given by tender.
Is this amount additional to what they are already receiving, or a new item?
It is to carry on the contract during the period of the winter months.
It is a different contract, is it not?
Yes.

There has been some agitation in Vancouver-and I presume it has come to the minister's notice-amongst a number of unemployed white seamen. They say: Why cannot these subsidized steamers employ whites exclusively? I have not at the moment the figures before me, but I was astonished to find the numbers of orientals that are employed on these boats running out of Vancouver, all of which are more or less subsidized on this line or carrying mail. I think the number of orientals ran up into several thousands; I think it was 5,000, if my memory serves me aright, although I would not care to guarantee that. They ask in these distressful times if, instead of taking up their crews in China, they could not take on British residents in Canada. Is the minister able to undertake any relief in that regard?

These ships employ, in regard to all the engine crews, officers and so on, only Canadians or other British subjects. It is only the portion of the crew comprising deck hands and stokers that is Chinese.
I Mr. Irvine.]
That is the majority, of course.
It is quite a story, and I do not desire to delay the committee by discussing the matter tonight, but if we leave it until the main estimates come up I shall discuss it.

Like the hon. member for Comox-Albemi I am also in receipt of many representations on this point. I should like to urge the government to look into this matter carefully, especially in regard to companies receiving subventions from the government of Canada. In that case I think the entire crew should be white.
May I say to my hon. friend very frankly that what is asked cannot be done for the money we are giving. The answer is this: It is a case of do it in the way it is being done or not at all.
Item agreed to.
Unemployment relief-further amount required, $975,000.

Many
hon. members have received representations expressing dissatisfaction, especially in my province of British Columbia, in regard to the scale of rates. May I ask the Minister of Pensions and National Health if a new scale for the winter has been satisfactorily established?
Mr. MadLAREN: The scale on which unemployment relief is granted for pensioners is that the amount of relief to those who are entitled to receive it is not less than the amount that is allowed by the municipality in which the individual resides. The matter is carefully scrutinized, and if an advance is made, especially during the winter, in any municipality, the amount under the department is raised to correspond with that. That is the policy for the winter months.
When does the minister expect to have the report of the committee in regard to pensions headed by Mr. Justice Rinfret?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Not before February. It will be during the remainder of the session.

May I ask, Mr. Chairman, if under this heading of unemployment relief there can be made any acknow-legment of or reference to the speech of the Minister of Labour recently concluded? His remarks included a very strong indictment of the hon. member for North Battleford with respect to soldier settlement.

Supply-Pensions

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Certainly unemployment relief can be discussed.

The Minister of
Labour made a very wide and slashing attack against the whole western contingent of Liberal members. He accused us of maligning our country and doing all kinds of things derogatory to our own interest. Mr. Speaker left the chair too quickly or I should have replied at that time, but since you are good enough to permit a reply now, I shall not say anything about the other matter. Two years ago the Prime Minister used to indulge in that sort of accusation, but I think he has got enough in return from this side of the house to feel he should discontinue it. Moreover he has been reformed in that respect and he took advantage of a certain event that occurred in this chamber to say something himself about conditions, not only in the west but throughout Canada. With your permission, Mr. Chairman, I would like to quote some of the Prime Minister's remarks on that occasion.
From what is the hon. member quoting?

I am quoting from
the report of the Imperial economic conference, the deliberations of which were held in this very chamber, and I should like to mention incidentally that we are not now in the Imperial conference but in the parliament of Canada and we are not to be cowed as the Prime Minister tried to bully the other delegates on that occasion. This is what he said:
Canada, like all other countries, has suffered severely from the calamitous fall in commodity prices. Since August, 1929, our index of wholesale prices has fallen 32 per cent and is now only four per cent above the prewar level. This means that the dollar has increased in purchasing power by 48 per cent. As a result of this rapid and persistent decline in the general price level and the inevitable disparities created between different kinds of prices, normal business relationships have been disrupted, profit margins have disappeared in many cases, enterprise has been discouraged, unemployment has steadily increased, the fiscal problems of all our public bodies have been greatly aggravated, and the burden of fixed charges is exerting an almost intolerable pressure upon some of the strategic elements in our national economy.
The author of that is the present Prime Minister of Canada. He continues:
Moreover, such fixed charges, except as they are reduced by bankruptcy and reorganization, are not being adjusted by the normal corrective processes which falling prices are supposed to set in motion. Indeed it seems that new dis-equilibria are created almost as rapidly as old
maladjustments are corrected and the paralysis of business enterprise with profit margins uncertain or non-existent continues. Trade languishes and unemployment persists or tends to become aggravated.
That is what the Prime Minister said during this conference held in this chamber. Let me continue:
I have said enough to indicate the importance which Canada is bound to place upon the solution of the problems of price instability and of unstable exchanges. In particular we believe that it is imperatively necessary to put a stop to the persistent decline in commodity prices which is paralysing private enterprise, choking off international trade, multiplying unemployment and social distress, and menacing the stability of our present social and economic order.
What hon. gentleman on this side spoke more strongly about conditions in Canada? I want to state that not one-half the truth has been told regarding conditions in the west. We scarcely breathe about the conditions to each other, much less to this chamber, and when any hon. gentleman opposite takes a different stand and pretends to know more about conditions than we do, he is getting beyond his depth and is talking of some thing of which he knows nothing. I have to compliment the Prime Minister on the great reform which has come over him in that respect. We remember quite well when he said that conditions in the west were due to our own extravagance and our speculating in the markets. By the way, he has done a little bit of market speculating himself, but we will come to that on a later item. He has been permanently cured, however. If the Minister of Labour wants to discipline anybody for talking honestly about conditions in the west I think he had better discipline his own leader, because he spoke more plainly with respect to Canadian conditions in this document that he gave to the world than we have ever done here.

Item agreed to.
Trade and Commerce-The Canada Grain Act, including management operation, maintenance and equipment of elevators, administration of 

further amount required, $100,009.

I gave notice, Mr. Chairman, that I wanted some more information about this marketing business. The Prime Minister made a very excellent statement the other day. I do not know whether anybody understood it or whether he himself did, but he left the impression on me that he was doing something for the farmers by way of supporting the market in lieu of paying the bonus on wheat which has been suspended this year. I have looked over the Prime Min-
Supply-Canada Grain Act

ister's statement very carefully since then, and I find that in three or four places he spoke deliberately of steadying the market, or putting some muscle into it, as the saying is, in lieu of paying the bonus this year. Answering a question by the hon. member for West Edmonton, the right hon. leader of the government indicated that this holding up of the market which he spoke of had been done since 1930. So there is no question of its having been done then in lieu of paying the bonus.
I should like a further explanation of that from my right hon. friend or from the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and while they are answering they might also tell us what was done with that wheat when they took it over from the pool by the selling agency which has been under Mr. McFarland's administration for the last two years or more. Was it sold directly as cash wheat, or held and storage paid on it, or converted into long range futures; and was more purchased? Further, why did not the government get out from under this wheat marketing business when they could get out at a profit? I understood the Prime Minister to say that there was a time when a profit could have been made on the pool wheat taken over by Mr. McFarland had the wheat been sold at that time. Unless my right hon. friend has some justification for holding that wheat we shall have to conclude that he was just like any other speculator and did not know when to let go. The government had an inquiry made some time ago, headed by Sir Josiah Stamp, into the wisdom and usefulness or otherwise of the market for futures. The commission evidently concluded that the futures market served some useful purpose. The pool made some mistakes, possibly, while they were handling this wheat. They were accused of gambling in wheat and of holding wheat when they should have sold. Mr. McFarland and the government, we are told by the Prime Minister, could have sold this wheat at a profit at one time. Possibly the right hon. gentleman will say that the government had nothing to do with the selection of Mr. McFarland, that the pools elected him, but he was recommended by the government and the pool only nominally appointed him. Mr. McFarland has now had charge of the selling agency for two years. He took it over with the idea that he was going to show the farmers how to engage in futures profitably. He engaged in trading in futures; it is admitted that he could have made a profit at one time he did not sell, and now he must admit a loss if sale were made

at present. I am ready to listen, and listen very carefully, to an explanation by either the Minister of Trade and Commerce or his leader the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I did not come prepared, Mr. Chairman, to discuss this matter tonight. It does not arise out of this item, which is to extend the facilities required by reason of a larger crop being reaped than was anticipated. But I may say this to the hon. gentleman, who is familiar with conditions in western Canada. I said that there was a blackboard loss when Mr. McFarland took over the operations of the pool. I said that there was a day or there were several days on which, if the wheat could have been sold, it could have been sold at a profit, but the difficulty was that it could not be sold. That has always been the difficulty; you had to let the farmer either sell or not sell for himself. As I say, Mr. Chairman, I did not bring any papers with me with which to meet questions of this kind, because I did not think on an item to provide facilities under the Canada Grain Act this matter could possibly be discussed. On mature consideration the hon. gentleman will see that it is hardly fair to expect this matter to be discussed on an item of this character.

Last year, Mr. Chairman, it was discussed on this very same item relating to the Canada Grain Act, and not only that, but we had the denial that Mr. McFarland was in the business of buying any kind of wheat. It is admitted now, but it was not admitted then.

Last year, I brought
up this very question of trading in wheat futures by Mr. McFarland, and I was told at that time that he was not trading in futures; that all he was handling was the wheat held by the pool, and that outside of that he had no activities whatever and was not hedging or buying futures.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
This discussion is out
of order on this item respecting the administration of "The Canada Grain Act, including management, operation, maintenance and equipment of elevators."

We discussed
the matter on this item before, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Yes, by consent of the house an item was reserved for discussion of all matters pertaining to the department.

Supply-Canada Grain Act

There is not another
item in the whole estimates under which you could discuss it except the item for the Canada Grain Act, and it was discussed on that item last year.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is quite right, but that was done by special consent. I remember very well, because I was in the chair at the time, that one item was reserved for a general discussion of all matters pertaining to the department. But if the committee agrees to the discussion continuing, I have no objection.

The Prime Minister left the impression on me that there was only one prop to the market this year, and that was Mr. McFarland, the representative of the pool and of the government, if you like to put it that way, and that had that prop been taken away the whole business would have come tumbling down like Samson when he got his hair cut. As we are only part of this world and as Winnipeg is only one of many wheat markets, has some great economic Goliath been holding up the markets in the rest of the world that there should be a parity in all markets at this time and that our market should not be out of line with the other markets in Antwerp, Rotterdam, London, Liverpool, Manchester, Chicago and Buenos Aires? Where are these Goliaths? Why should my right hon. friend take all the credit for holding up the world's market at this time particularly when the market fell so badly? That is what he did, Mr. Chairman in his recent statement, and I could quote his words to you, but you would not let me; you never do. But it is in Hansard in black and white. I am not going to say that the Prime Minister deliberately deceived us. I do not think he knows much more about the market than I do, and I do not pretend to be an expert. I am searching for information, and if I have to depend on my right hon. friend I am afraid it will be a case of the blind leading the blind, unless he divulges more than he did on the recent occasion to which I have reference. I am not joking. I want to know if it is true that the wheat market not only in Canada but all over the world was kept either up or down during this period to which we have reference this year by the right hon. leader of the government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The answer to that is
no.

No to what? This is what the right hon. gentleman said on November 14:
Under . these circumstances, Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited-
That is the company which this government was behind:

to which I have referred, became the only available hedging organization left in western Canada, and the government is faced at the moment with the issue as to whether or not, under these circumstances, it would give its support as provided by the Relief Act passed in 1931 and 1932 as well.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is right.

There was no other hedging avenue. My information is to the effect that every elevator company, inside of twenty-four hours after they buy in the country, have their grain purchases hedged. It is because the pool had not their grain hedged two years or so ago that they suffered a loss. The rest of them had theirs hedged, and yet my right hon. friend takes the ground that he is the hedger for the whole grain trade. That is what he says.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: As I have indicated, Mr. Chairman, I am not in a position to discuss this matter because I did not bring a single note with me, being under the impression that this question would not be reconsidered. There will be ample opportunity when the estimates are before the house to discuss the matter fully. I repeat that the only available hedging possible is that provided by the wheat seller, by this organization.
They hedge for the trade as well.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: They did some for the trade. I said the other day that I was not quite certain. However, I inquired about it, and found that they did some hedging.
They did all the hedging?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No.
There was hedging on our Canadian market of Chicago wheat as well. Were they doing the buying of this wheat also?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I cannot answer, because I have not the papers before me.

I came unprepared
also, because I did not expect the Prime Minister to be present. He seldom is when these questions are under discussion. The Minister of Trade and Commerce spoke last year, because it comes under his department.
Supply-Canada Grain Act

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: He has not his information before him, either.

He made quite
different answers last year. I will not press it too hard, because there might have been state reasons for his answering other than exactly correctly. I am ready to forgive that. But when it is admitted by the Prime Minister this year that the government was in the wheat market I think it is high time we knew the facts.

In view of what the
Prime Minister has just said, namely that he has not the information before him, and in view of the fact that we have attempted on many occasions during the last seven weeks to extract from the government their position in connection with the wheat problem, will the Prime Minister give a guarantee to the house that when this matter comes up again for discussion the information will be given?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The word "guarantee" is a highly improper term to use. I will say, however, that so far as the government is concerned it will supply any information it has at its disposal if the house, or the committee of the house, and the opposition, think it is in the public interest to ask it. I will put the full responsibility for it exactly where it belongs.
Until we do get this information we won't know whether the government has helped or hurt the market this year.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The Premier of Alberta made that perfectly clear. The other day Mr. Brownlee said what we had done had saved the situation, and I believe he is as well informed in these matters as any other gentleman in western Canada. I presume hon. members opposite saw his public statement in that regard. I know only this, that if we had to do it over again we would do exactly as we did.
Yes, we see statements; there is always someone ready to make them when they are required. Statements are always forthcoming when it is necessary to prop up the government as well as the market.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I may say I had no
knowledge of what Mr. Brownlee was going to say.
Did the Premier of Alberta have information when he made that statement?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: What is that?

Did he have information
when he made that statement?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I have had no communication with him. It was made after the statement made by me in the house the other day.

Last year I brought this matter up, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce told me the government had not taken any action of the kind. Now the Prime Minister tells us that they have been in the market since 1930. I was in this house in 1928, 1929 and 1930. We were told how the pools had been gambling in wheat, and it was because they had gambled that they had made such great losses. Last year and the year before I listened to the Prime Minister tell us that the reason the farmers in western Canada were so hard up was that they had been playing the stock market. Now we find that the big boy is going to show us how he gambled in wheat. It seems we have been in it for two or three years, but we have not had a statement yet. We do not know whether we are behind or whether we are ahead. When I suggest that there might be a profit the Prime Minister says that if there is any profit it goes to the bank.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I did not say any such
thing. Mr. Chairman, I ask that the hon. member retract that statement.

I beg the right hon.
gentleman's pardon; I meant to the selling agency.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Thank you.

The suggestion that
there was a profit was rather outside the question. One day we were told they were ahead of the market, that if they sold out and cleared up they would be ahead. speakeroldname: Hon. W. A. GORDON (Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, with the consent of the house I should like to table the answer to a question appearing as No. 33 in the votes and proceedings of November 23, 1932. The question was asked by Mr. Bourgeois, and I think the information should be tabled as soon as possible. The question and answer are as follows:

1.	With respect to the return to the land movement, how many persons in the province of Quebec have benefited by the provisions of the Unemployment and Farm Relief Act and received assistance from the federal government up to the present time?
2.	How many persons in each of the other provinces of Canada have benefited thereby and been similarly assisted?

1.	The provincial government of Quebec reports that up to date 148 families with 768 dependents, making a total of 916 individuals, have been settled under the relief settlement plan in accordance with the terms of the agreement entered into between the federal government and the province of Quebec under the provisions of The Relief Act, 1932, and that approximately 375 additional families are expected to be settled this season.
2.	The provincial government of Nova Scotia reports 95 settlers placed on the land with 522 dependents, making a total of 617 individuals to November 1st, 1932. In addition a further 22 applications have been approved by the province.
The provincial government of Ontario reports 226 settlers placed on the land with 932 dependents, making a total of 1,158 individuals to October 5th, 1932.
The provincial government of Manitoba reports 179 settlers placed on the land with 637 dependents, making a total of 816 individuals to November 7th, 1932.
The provincial government of Saskatchewan reports 366 settlers placed on the land with 1,313 dependents, making a total of 1,679 individuals to October 18th, 1932, and that a further 133 additional settlers have been selected for settlement.
The provincial government of Alberta reports that 29 families with 108 dependents making a total of 137 individuals have been approved by the province for settlement.
